Why Thinking More Can Make an LLM Dumb

ByteByteGo
Nov 17
 
READ IN APP
 

How much of your week is spent answering questions? (Sponsored)

New hires, support, PMs, and your coding agents all need to know how the product works and why it works that way. Today, you’re the one pointing them in the right direction.

Unblocked works out what’s current and relevant across your code, PRs, tickets, Slack, and production data, so:

  • Everyone gets cited answers in Slack without pulling in an engineer

  • When the answer turns into a fix, a cloud agent drafts the PR

  • Your agents generate code that follows past decisions, no steering needed

See how it works

When you ask someone to double-check an answer, you usually expect that you’ll get a better answer.

For example, when we look at an invoice the second time, we might find out that an item was counted twice. However, the opposite experience is also quite common. You might revisit a straightforward question on an exam and convince yourself that there’s a catch. In this case, you might end up changing an answer that was correct the very first time.

A reasoning language model can do both. It might use extra time to catch a mistake, or it can also use that time to develop a wrong interpretation. Both scenarios come from a basic feature of language models. Once a model writes down an idea, you can build on that idea a few steps later. But whether it improves the answer or gets things wrong depends on the original question.

In this article, we’ll try to understand why thinking longer can make an LLM dumber. Here’s what we’ll cover:

  • How a language model builds on its answers

  • What happens before a reasoning model sends a reply

  • The advantage of extra time on a question

  • How to teach a model to use extra steps

  • When the model has already done enough

  • How an extra step turns a right answer into a wrong one

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

How a Language Model Builds on its Own Words

An LLM generates text in small pieces called tokens. You can think of a token as a word, part of a word, or a symbol. When the model selects its next token, it takes the original question into consideration along with the text it has already generated. This means that whatever the model writes near the start of an answer can have a big impact on the calculations it does multiple sentences later.

Let’s say you have a shop that raises the price of a $100 item by 20% and then reduces the new price by 20%. What’s the final price? Without too much thinking, you might be tempted to say $100. This is because the percentage values look the same, and the words “raises” and “reduces” seem to cancel each other out.

But as you might’ve guessed, such an answer would be incorrect. The final price is $96. And the best way to get to this answer in a systematic manner is to write down the intermediate answer. Or the answer to the first calculation, which should be $120. This makes it easy to calculate the price after a 20% reduction.

An LLM can also benefit from the same sequence of checking the intermediate results. Once it has found out that the new price is $120, it can easily calculate the price after the discount. You can see that the question has been broken into smaller ones and carried the result of the first answer into the second. Such a sequence of steps is also known as a chain of thought. In this example, the most useful part of the chain is a single number that makes it easy to handle the next calculation.

What Happens Before a Reasoning Model Replies?

An ordinary LLM can provide a fully worked solution when you ask it to explain a calculation step by step. However, reasoning models such as OpenAI’s o1 were specifically trained to generate intermediate work before generating a final answer. Even if you ask for just the final price, a reasoning model can work through the price change before returning the final answer.

Most LLMs use a type of neural network called a Transformer. One of the abilities of the Transformer-based model is to connect the text that it is currently generating with relevant parts of the text that was generated earlier. This basic design approach can handle both a quick reply and a longer calculation. With their model, DeepSeek also showed how further training could teach an existing Transformer-based model to use this ability of intermediate results much more effectively.

You can think of the intermediate results working as a sort of scratchpad. Let’s say you give a model 3 different calendars of people and ask for the earliest half-hour when everyone is free. The final answer might be “Tuesday at 11.” But before generating that answer, the model is going to compare the calendars, find out that an earlier slot works for only two people, and then move on to the next available slot. The answer might take just a few words. But the work that happens behind the scenes is much more than that.

The tokens that are used for this work are often called reasoning tokens or thinking tokens. Many model providers keep the raw reasoning of their models private and might just display a summary so that the user might think of the work that was done in the background as mainly a pause of some sort. Sometimes a reasoning trace of a model might look like a conversation between two people because one sentence proposes an idea and a later one objects to it. A single model might be generating both sentences.

The Advantage of Extra Time on a Difficult Question

There are two main times when you can spend computing power on a model.

First is at the time of training, when the model adjusts its internal settings based on examples or feedback. These changes can have a big impact on how the model answers future questions.

Second is at the time of inference. At that time, the trained model uses the settings made at the time of training to answer the question in front of it. If you spend more computing power on that individual request, it is called inference-time scaling. Also known as test-time scaling.

Let’s say you have a piece of code that’s supposed to process every item in a list. It numbers the items starting from one and keeps running while the current position is less than the total number of items in the list. Now, imagine that a user complains that the last item always goes missing. A model might immediately think that the stopping condition of the loop might have a problem. That’s a pretty reasonable guess, and there is a simple way to test it.

With three items, the loop goes to positions one and two. When it goes to position three, the condition checks whether 3 is less than 3. The answer is false, and so the loop stops before processing the third item. Simply the act of following the code through a small example can turn a possible suspicion into a final explanation. It also shows that making the loop run when the two numbers are equal would fix this bug.

This is one way to spend extra time. Within a single attempt, you can have each step build on what the previous step found out. Another approach is to come up with several separate solutions and compare their final answers. However, separate attempts can help more each attempt can make different mistakes. In contrast, a longer individual attempt is much more beneficial when you let the model follow a promising idea long enough to verify it.

How To Teach A Model to Use Extra Steps

How can a model learn that checking its work can pay off?

For reference, DeepSeek explored this with their R1-Zero model. The team started with a pretrained model that had already learned patterns of language, code, and mathematics. This was followed by the use of reinforcement learning. The model attempted problems, received scores for its responses, and gradually adjusted what kind of responses it was likely to generate.

Some problems benefit from this approach because you can check their answers automatically. For example, in the case of a math question with a known result, a program can easily compare the model’s answers with an answer key. For a coding problem, you can have tests that show what works and what doesn’t. A different solution might pass both cases. But the tests can differentiate between the two even if both come with convincing explanations.

DeepSeek used a training method called Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

The idea behind this method is that for a question, the model generates a group of attempts. Some might solve the problem directly. Some might fix an earlier mistake. Others might give the wrong answer. The training procedure can score each attempt and compare its score with those of the other attempts. Once that’s done, you can adjust the model to favor attempts that work better than their peers.

There are two jobs over here.

One is where you grade an actual attempt. The other is when you estimate what score an attempt might ordinarily get so that the training procedure has something to compare things to.

Some reinforcement learning methods also train a separate model, known as the critic model, to provide that estimate. GRPO gets its comparison from the group’s own scores. The R1-Zero model made use of these rules to grade correctness and to check whether the response followed the proper format. This allowed the system to recognize a successful attempt even when nobody had written out the particular route the model took to solve it.

During training, DeepSeek looked at an intermediate version of the R1-Zero model working on an equation that had square roots. The model squared both sides and began developing a more complicated expression. However, in the middle, it stopped that approach and came back to the original equation to reconsider what it had done. Partway through, it interrupted that approach, returned to the original equation, and reconsidered its steps. The team thought of this as an “aha moment.”

The interesting bit for them was where the decision to go back had come from. The team had given a problem, a place where the model could write the working solution, and a way to score the result. This had left the choice of strategy to the model. Yet at a particular point in the calculation, the model came up with a response that considered one of its own steps worth looking at again.

You can probably see why this behavior can be so useful over many practice problems.

An attempt that continues after making an early mistake might carry that mistake all the way to the answer. An attempt that reconsiders the questionable step has a good chance to recover and get a better score. The feedback applies to the attempt as a whole. Therefore, you can also have a lucky guess that also earns credits. However, across many different problems, such a strategy has more advantages.

This was DeepSeek’s experiment in going directly from a pretrained model to reinforcement learning. For the released DeepSeek-R1, the team also used examples. R1-Zero sometimes switched languages or produced solutions that were hard to follow. Therefore, the team began R1 with supervised fine-tuning, which meant training on examples of desired responses.

When the Model Has Already Done Enough

The first form of overthinking is easy to overlook because the user still receives a correct answer.

However, in a study of reasoning models, researchers showed what can happen when one model was asked to calculate “2 + 3”. It arrived at five in its first solution, then continued until its response contained thirteen solutions to the same question. Nearly all of that text appeared after the calculation had already been done correctly.

Why would a model keep going even when it had the correct answer?

Think about how an attempt is scored. If you have two responses that use the required format and both end in 5, a checker dealing with correctness can give them the same score. You might have one response that stops after a short calculation. The other response might count objects, reverse the order of addition. Both arrive at the right answer. The score offers little guidance about which response made better use of the user’s time.

If you have a check that confirms an answer, it can still be valuable. Let’s say you calculate the total for an order and then compare the items that were counted with the original order form. Even if you confirm the total, that comparison could have shown that an item was missing. If you simply add the numbers from our own incomplete list a second time, you are much less likely to catch that particular error. What matters is whether the second pass tests something the first one could have missed.

This shows why knowing when to stop is a separate skill. A user with an answer key can look back and point to the first correct result. However, a model that answers a new question usually has to decide if another check is worth it before it knows how the answer will be judged. On a difficult problem, if the model stops at the first plausible result, it can be quite costly. But on an easy one, the habit of checking again can produce a long wait for an answer, which is unnecessary.

How an Extra Step Turns a Right Answer Into a Wrong One

The “2 +3” example shows the impact of wasted effort. However, you can also run into a different problem when the extra reasoning brings in an incorrect assumption. For example, let’s say you have a question about the train departure time printed on the timetable. A train is scheduled to leave at 9:00, but it usually leaves 10 minutes late.

The timetable gives the time as 9:00. Let’s say that the model identifies that answer immediately, but continues because the point about the delay sounds too deliberate to ignore. It might come to the conclusion that the train will probably leave at 9:10. It may even produce a sensible explanation about the difference between scheduled and actual departures. If it finally answers 9:10, the calculation is correct. But the model has gone from its core task of reporting what the timetable says to trying to predict when the train will leave.

As you can see, the original question is still available to the model. What has changed is the text it can use to form the final answer. Early in the response, simply telling the scheduled time from the timetable is the obvious candidate. Later, the model has also produced a second answer and multiple sentences that try to explain why that time might be important. While each sentence makes sense, the response drifts away from what was intended from the model. To a casual user, the answer might even appear dumb.

This is also important when looking at the relation between thinking time and accuracy. If longer answers contain more errors, one possibility is that the model wrote longer because those questions were harder to begin with. A better comparison is to give the same model the same questions with different amounts of reasoning capability. On difficult questions, the extra steps may catch mistakes. But on straightforward questions, they may repeat a simple conclusion or end up providing an irrelevant detail that’s enough to change the answer.

References:

  • Learning to reason with LLMs

  • DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

Inference engineering for software engineers

When is the right time to drop APIs provided by the frontier AI labs, and what about choosing models & providers, caching, dedicated GPUs, KV cache concerns, and more? A practical deepdive

Gergely Orosz and Ivan Klaric
Nov 17
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

A recent trend we’ve covered is of tech companies moving to open models to rein in AI spend: Uber cut its per-token costs by 50%, Pinterest by 90%, and even AT&T has achieved a 56% decrease. But how do you move from a frontier lab’s APIs to using open models? There are two options:

  • “Bare metal:” With plenty of time and money, you can go “bare metal” and purchase a few dozen NVIDIA GPUs and use those AI supercomputers, like Revolut has done: running 56 separate B200 units itself to serve its inference needs. This is a lot of work to set it up, but after that, operational costs are as cheap as it gets.

  • Inference provider: most companies contract with an inference provider that operates large fleets of GPUs, and makes it easy for customers to onboard and start using open models fast.

Onboarding to an inference provider to run LLM workloads comes with challenges, such as dealing with tail latencies, worrying about cache hit rates, rate limits, and more. Inference engineering is a set of engineering practices that we believe is increasingly beneficial for software engineers to familiarize themselves with. To go deeper into this area, we’ve talked with three leading inference providers to learn more: Modal, Fireworks AI, and Baseten. Today, we cover:

  1. What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs? They have GPU infrastructure similar to frontier labs, don’t train their own frontier models and are experts at hosting open models.

  2. When to switch from frontier labs? The most common reasons are to reduce costs, have more control over latency, and to fine-tune AI models.

  3. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy. Use evals to find the right open model for your use case, evaluate vendors, and decide between multi-tenant API usage and dedicated GPUs.

  4. Stage #1: API replacement using a multi-tenant inference setup. The easiest way to onboard to an inference provider is to “swap” the API of a frontier lab to an API of an inference provider. But there may be latency problems and caching issues at high loads.

  5. Signs you’ve outgrown multi-tenant inference APIs. Hitting rate limits, performance consistency problems, and overpaying for usage are signs that it might be time to adopt dedicated GPUs.

  6. Stage #2: Configuring dedicated GPU nodes. With dedicated GPUs, you’ll need to get into the details: size of the model, interactivity versus throughput, KV cache sizing, failover options, and more.

  7. Speculative decoding. If there’s unused compute during the decode phase, you might consider a Speculator to further boost inference performance.

As usual, we have no affiliation with vendors mentioned in this article, and have not been paid to mention any company. Special thanks to Richard Gong (Inference lead, Modal), Dmytro Dzhulgakov (cofounder and CTO, Fireworks), and Philip Kiely (Special Projects at Baseten) for sharing details about inference engineering challenges.

The bottom of this article could be cut off in some email clients. Read the full article uninterrupted, online.

Read the full article online

1. What are inference providers & how do they differ from AI labs?

Inference providers are companies that sell access to LLMs which they run on users’ behalf. From the outside, this isn’t so different to what OpenAI and Anthropic offer: an API endpoint, ability to stream tokens, and pay based on token usage.

But what makes inference providers different from frontier labs is the models running behind the endpoint: inference providers run open-weight models, whereas frontier labs train their own models. In this field, Modal, Fireworks, and Baseten each operate slightly different strategies:

  • Modal sees itself as a cloud infrastructure provider that focuses on making its offering programmable via its SDKs. It natively supports inference services through its SDKs, but leans heavily on the open source ecosystem for running its inference workloads efficiently. Performance tweaks to its stack are merged upstream. In the words of Richard Gong, Inference Lead at Modal: “when you run code on Modal, you should be able to see all the code that’s running.”

  • Fireworks positions itself as a provider for specialized AI workloads. Most of its business is in dedicated deployments, which often include fine-tuning and provision of latency guarantees. Much fine-tuning and post-training is available for self-service. Fireworks also offers forward-deployed researchers that can help with post-training custom models or components. Dmytro Dzhulgakov, Fireworks’ CTO, says: “our tagline is specialized intelligence, which means we will tune everything from model to infrastructure for your particular use case.”

  • Baseten describes itself as an all-in-one place to build agents. It starts with the basic infrastructure layer with uptime guarantees, flexible commercial terms, without vendor lock-in. Baseten builds additional layers for building agentic workloads on top of its inference platform. These additional layers include sandboxes, governance services, and self-serving, post-training functionality.

To customers, inference providers offer LLM APIs that can be used as drop-in replacements for frontier labs’ APIs. However, inference providers are not the same, as suggested above:

  1. Inference providers don’t pre-train their own foundational models. A single pre-training run for frontier-level LLMs can cost millions of dollars, and only hyperscalers and specialized frontier labs can afford it. Inference providers run post-training on open-weight models because it’s significantly cheaper.

  2. Competitive pricing. The main business of inference providers is offering open-weight models at competitive rates.

  3. Dedicated hardware. A big part of the appeal of inference providers is the ability to have dedicated hardware for users to interact with vendors on the infrastructure layer.

  4. Efficiency & customization. Inference providers offer similar commoditized open models, and compete heavily on efficiency and customization services.

As an example of efficiency, Fireworks announced its Ember-1 model in September 2026, that is post-trained on the Kimi K3 foundation, delivering a similar quality level but with 40% fewer reasoning tokens consumed. Consuming far fewer reasoning tokens gives Fireworks an edge on cost compared to a vanilla Kimi K3 model.

In general, frontier labs have poor uptime, and this helps inference vendors win market share. API Uptime provided by frontier labs isn’t at the levels expected of modern cloud providers: currently, the self-declared uptime of Anthropic is 99.5%, and for OpenAI it’s 99.97% for API, and 99.2% for ChatGPT. These numbers are well below the four nines (99.99%+) uptime expected of cloud providers – which is something that a vendor like AWS is known to uphold.

Imagine you’re a developer aiming to provide a 99.99% uptime guarantee for your application; you can’t rely on a single frontier LLM provider for the service’s critical path. But in the graphs above, degraded performance slots aren’t counted as downtime. As all these APIs are multi-tenant, it means that performance degradations will naturally hit some tenants – with no way to be aware of the degradation, or do anything about it.

Reliability is an ongoing concern with the LLMs of frontier providers and inference providers. Even though many inference vendors offer higher reliability guarantees than frontier models, inference providers can also go down, too. For companies that use inference providers, it’s common to use an LLM gateway with fallback logic to another provider – or to a frontier API. We explored this in a deepdive with Ramp, whose LLM router project started with this exact problem statement.

2. When to switch from frontier labs?

Moving from frontier AI labs to an independent inference provider is often driven by three factors: cost, control, and the need for more customization.

Most common reason: cost

Many companies start considering inference providers because they have pressing cost concerns. In many cases, a frontier model is more capable than necessary for most requests, meaning a “dumber” model is just as good for simpler tasks – and nobody would notice the difference! In such cases, it’s a “no-brainer” for an engineering team to choose to route some requests to a cheaper model hosted by an inference provider.

“Smart routing” is an obvious way to cut costs. An LLM router – the “smart router” – is prompt-aware and can route an LLM request to the most cost-efficient provider that can solve the request. This is an approach that fuelled Uber’s ~50% cut in per-token costs this summer.

Providers offer OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible API endpoints, so switching providers is trivial. All that is needed is to point your app at the new endpoint operated by a “smart router.”

But how to decide which model to serve? Generic benchmarks are often insufficient because they usually do not fully represent a team’s traffic patterns. Most inference providers ask for prompt samples or eval sets in order to gauge which model best serves a customer’s use case. The experience of using a new LLM endpoint resembles using APIs provided by frontier labs, while API calls are still charged per token, and response time SLAs generally don’t exist.

More control over latency

When you use a frontier lab’s endpoint, there is little control over operational issues like response latency and model availability. Opting for a dedicated setup with an inference provider offers full control over both:

  • Latency: model response times are more predictable because the app has dedicated capacity that can scale by usage.

  • Model availability: Engineers can run the model of their choosing on their dedicated GPUs and keep operating it as long as needed, avoiding the risk of a frontier lab changing models from one day to the next.

Fine-tuning model quality: customization

When an inference stack runs on dedicated hardware with open source models, it’s possible to work with inference providers to finetune a model’s quality as required, which optimizes latency or throughput performance. Richard Gong of Modal says that around 10% of their customers go this far, suggesting that customization is for “power users”.

Fine-tuning a model’s quality is typical in two scenarios:

  • Tweaking a smaller model: achieving a similar level of quality with a smaller model, with fewer parameters. This performance gain is achieved via performance tweaks not possible with off-the-shelf models. Inference providers allow you to post-train a smaller model for your specific use case. A post-trained small model can then outperform the original model in those specialized scenarios.

  • Fine tuning for niche use cases. Improving quality when general purpose models aren’t good enough, often because the data isn’t publicly available. For example, projects in the legal and medical sectors tend to benefit from this, according to the Fireworks team.

3. Choosing a model, provider, and deployment strategy

Most inference providers offer the exact same models to run, and the differences lie in model performance and quality. For example, model quality can differ by default context length, and some providers cap this to below what the model supports. There’s also quantization to consider, where a model’s weights are compressed to a lower numerical precision, or default temperature aka controlling how random the output is. Here’s a practical approach for selecting a provider:

  1. Model: Choose an AI model to switch to

  2. Provider: pick an inference provider to host the model, based on model quality, performance, and cost

  3. Deployment model: decide whether to use a multi-tenant service, or to move to dedicated GPU nodes

Choosing a model

The most obvious way to decide which model to use is to run an eval set against the various model options. In the latest episode of The Pragmatic Engineer Podcast, Microsoft’s CEO Satya Nadella argues that private evals shall be a big component of tech companies’ intellectual property (IP) in the future. He says:

“Public benchmarks are great, but your private evals will matter more: you need your own eval for the outcome that matters to you. Then you look at performance across all these models and continuously optimize.

Our customers start with a frontier model, then say: ‘I’ve got all those traces. This is a deterministic workflow, so I don’t need the next big model drop. I want to optimize the cost.’ They drop in [another] model, use the traces to fine-tune it – and there you have it.”

An example of public benchmarks is from Artificial Analysis that maintains an eval set to compare costs for generic tasks across different models. Here are the average costs per task, broken down by model:

Let’s say you build an app on top of Anthropic’s Sonnet 5.5 model, costing $5.46 on average per task in the index. If Kimi K3 is sufficient for this use case, then that model is ~60% cheaper to run at only $2.00 per task. Note that the cost comparison here is per-task, not per-token. This makes sense because different models require different numbers of tokens to complete a task, which makes it harder to compare model costs without your own private evals!

Having said that, deciding whether a model is good enough requires more than just looking at public benchmark results. Ideally, there’s an eval set to compare models with. In the absence of that, running an A/B experiment is a good alternative. For example, if you want to switch agentic coding workflows to an inference provider, you could simply let some engineers use the new model and give feedback on the results.

Choosing a provider

All providers tweak open models to squeeze out more performance without degrading quality too much. Therefore, model outputs and quality vary among providers. A useful tool for comparing providers’ model accuracy is Artificial Analysis’ endpoint accuracy index. This is a score that benchmarks results from various inference providers against its own, self-hosted version. An index value of 100% means the provider’s results are the same as Artificial Analysis’ own hosted model.

Endpoint accuracy is broadly similar and the scores of providers range from 93% to 102%. The variance comes from performance and quality tweaks that inference providers make to their versions of open models. Since LLMs are non-deterministic, this measurement has a 95% confidence interval – which adds another layer of complexity to evaluation. Minor score differences are considered within the same level as Artificial Analysis’ reference model, hence the green coloring of bars that are technically below 100%.

Deployment model: multi-tenant or dedicated?

All providers’ offerings include a multi-tenant API, as well as dedicated GPUs to run LLMs. This deployment progression is typically a graduation path: most deployments start as drop-in API replacements of frontier labs’ APIs, and as usage grows they start switching to dedicated infrastructure.

When switching to an open model hosted by an inference provider, the per-token cost decreases. However, you are still running in a multi-tenant environment, which comes with similar performance bottlenecks, like when using the API endpoint of a frontier model. The difference is that with an inference provider, you can migrate to a dedicated hosting environment and have full control over a deployment’s performance. Having your own deployment (controlling the GPUs with the inference provider) makes it possible to fine-tune a model’s quality with techniques such as post-training.

Typical graduation path from multi-tenant API to dedicated GPUs

The most typical path for a startup using LLMs:

  1. Use a frontier lab’s API endpoints

  2. Move over to using an open model, using the API endpoint of an inference provider

  3. Rent dedicated GPUs from the inference provider

Moving to an inference provider is usually coupled with achieving some kind of product-market fit. All three inference providers we spoke with told us that by the time a customer signs up by getting to “stage 1” (see below), their product has gained traction in the market. Per-token costs only become important with non-trivial levels of user activity.

“Stage 2” with dedicated GPUs is a level that implies significant budget commitments, a more mature product, and large-scale usage.

Getting inference capacity: this can be tricky, given the global GPU shortage! We previously covered how there’s a CPU shortage inside cloud providers – and so there should be no surprise that there’s an even more pressing GPU shortage. Even large inference providers are having a hard time getting all the GPUs they need. The inference providers we talked with all run on top of several cloud providers – plus some also manage their own bare metal – exactly to get as much capacity as they can. Getting access to more GPUs justifies the added operational complexity from running in multiple clouds. Being able to quickly onboard new cloud providers that have spare capacity is becoming a key differentiator in the industry.

If you need dedicated GPUs, know that it will probably be expensive. Scarce capacity is one of the reasons why getting a dedicated setup typically requires long-term budget commitments upfront. To put it simply: you’ll need to pay a larger amount, and commit for paying for those GPUs on a longer timeframe.

4. Stage #1: API replacement, using a multi-tenant inference setup

For teams with hefty LLM bills, the easiest way to decrease cost is to replace frontier labs’ models in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, with a frontier-level open model. Looking at data from OpenCode and OpenRouter, the current most popular choices of engineering teams for this include DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3, and others including Kimi K3.1 Pro.

The easiest way to carry out a replacement is to point an application to an API provided by the inference provider. In practice, this means using a multi-tenant API where other customers will be hitting the same endpoint, similar to using an API endpoint from a frontier lab. At first, everything will be great, but then you may come across problems of time-to-first-token (TTFT) latency, caching-related costs, and latency issues.

These are also problems of using APIs from frontier labs, the difference being that with inference providers, there’s the option of solving most of them by moving over to a dedicated deployment.

Latency problems: TTFT, inference time, user-experienced latency

Time-to-first-token is a measure of how long it takes from the moment a request hits the LLM API, to when the client starts receiving the first tokens. The distribution of TTFT latencies has a long tail:

A long right tail means that a significant proportion of requests have double the median latency or longer. So, when measuring latencies, the p95/p99 latencies are just as important as p50 latencies. TTFT can be measured in two places:

  • Inference time: provider-instrumented TTFT shows the pure inference time. Some providers expose this metric to customers on dashboards, while some include it in their responses. Frontier labs typically do neither.

  • User-experienced latency: client-instrumented TTFT shows the full user-experienced latency, including things like network transport, or the TLS handshake.

Server-side inference is just one part of the overall time that an app’s user spends awaiting a response. To achieve truly fast p95 times for user latency, it’s best to consider optimizations like connection pooling on the LLM API consumer side.

When serving LLM APIs on shared infrastructure, inference providers run many copies of the LLM inference engine that serves customer requests. A single inference engine can serve multiple requests concurrently. A new replica is created when the number of concurrent requests exceeds the current replica capacity. Scaling of replicas is one reason why inference-only TTFT latencies vary so much.

Other reasons why TTFT can vary:

  1. ‘Noisy neighbour’ effects: a request is batched with another request that’s more expensive to process, so it takes longer than if the request was in a batch with a similar request.

  2. Cold start: happens when a request is waiting in a queue because there is no capacity in existing replicas. The inference provider is creating new replicas but this isn’t instantaneous, so a request has to wait until the new replica becomes available (until the new replica starts up, from a “cold”, offline state).

  3. Cold cache: when sending a large request for the first time, it may end up on a replica without the relevant KV cache loaded (the cache is “cold” – which is the opposite of “hot cache” when the KV cache is already populated). An inference provider will typically try to keep requests sticky to the same replica because that keeps replica’s KV cache hot. Sometimes, this isn’t possible because your cache expired, or it landed on the replica that doesn’t have the relevant KV cache. KV cache then has to either be copied from cold storage if available, or if it’s not, fully processed before the first token can be generated.

Prompt cache utilization is observable and actionable by engineers building on LLM APIs. You can get prompt cache utilization metrics from the response of the OpenAI completions API. Building your apps to effectively exploit prompt cache is a key technique in improving app performance, so it’s worth taking a closer look.

Caching issues: cost and latency

Most major LLM API endpoints today are stateless REST APIs, inspired by OpenAI’s chat completions API.

LLM endpoints are stateless, which creates problems because most LLM use cases are stateful. Dmytro Dzhulgakov, cofounder and CTO at Fireworks calls the decision to make the API stateless “the original sin” because while the client app behaves like it’s talking to a stateless API, the burden is on the provider to ensure efficient caching mechanisms in a distributed environment.

Here’s an example to illustrate the problems that stateless APIs cause: an app with user’s inputs, LLM prompts, and the agentic context layer:

The agentic context layer – the home of the business logic – is between the user and the LLM. This context layer injects conversation steering and tool usage logic by preparing the LLM prompt. The user’s input is only part of the prompt the LLM sees.

The two prompts the LLM sees in this example share a large common prefix: they only start diverging after 16 words: “you are a helpful coding agent that helps users learn python”. If those two LLM API calls end up on the same instance, the inference engine will be able to use the prompt cache and skip processing the first 16 words. Hooray!

When using the OpenAI-compatible completions API, it’s possible to monitor how many tokens in a request were cached. The API response contains a usage JSON object that contains two useful fields:

  • prompt_tokens: how many input tokens were in the request

  • prompt_token_details.cached_tokens: how many input tokens were fetched from cache

Cache hit ratio isn’t just important for performance reasons, it’s also a critical cost consideration. Let’s do some napkin math, starting with basic assumptions:

  • a token cost of $5 per 1M input tokens

  • 90% discount for cached tokens ($0.5 per 1M input tokens)

Processing 1M input tokens then costs:

So, if the cache hit rate drops from 99% to 90%, the cost of processing 1M input tokens grows 74%. If it drops to zero, it grows 10x!

Several warning messages inside of AI tools are related to token caching. Token caching is such a common cost reduction technique that Claude Code warns about low cache hit ratios from switching models mid-conversation:

The same happens inside Claude Desktop:

But why would the model cache be lost when switching from Opus to Fable, for example? It’s because models vary in architecture, so it’s not possible to share cache when switching models. If the architecture of the model were the same, the cache could be copied to a new machine, but with a different architecture, it needs to be re-built from scratch when switching models.

Switching to dedicated instances can help improve cache hits. If the cache hit ratio is stable – meaning you did a good job of reusing caches at the application layer – but there are still occasional spikes in p95 latencies and the provider occasionally moves workloads to fresh GPUs with no pre-loaded cache, then in this case, it’s probably time to consider switching to a dedicated instance setup with the inference provider in order to avoid p95 spikes.

5. Signs you’ve outgrown multi-tenant inference APIs

At some point, you may outgrow a multi-tenant inference setup, and there are signs to look out for when this stage is reached:

Rate limits

The most obvious sign is starting to get rate limited; typically by seeing certain HTTP responses:

  • HTTP 429: Too Many Requests. This is the standard rate limiting error. The client should retry with an exponential backoff.

  • HTTP 503: Service Unavailable or HTTP 529: Service Overloaded. These errors indicate that the client hasn’t done anything wrong, but the shared service it’s connecting to is overloaded and can’t process the request. Retrying might help, but since most other clients will also be retrying, it might make sense to fail over to a different provider.

Rate limits are expressed in two metrics:

  1. Requests per minute (RPM): how many calls to the endpoint can be made per minute

  2. Tokens per minute (TPM): the total number of tokens that a service sends per minute. Some providers differentiate between prompt, cached, and output tokens.

Here are differences in how providers enforce request limits in their multi-tenant, public API deployment:

In the case of Fireworks, TPM limits change dynamically with usage. The token limit grows by 25% at most every 15 minutes if more than half of the previous limit has been used. The dynamic limit similarly drops when not in use.

Elsewhere, Baseten has strict limits that can be raised as customers go to higher tiers. Modal, on the other hand, sets no explicit limits on RPMs or TPMs, but limits how many requests can be processed concurrently.

Performance consistency problems

The LLM latency from a shared API endpoint varies over the course of a day. This performance variance, (also called the noisy neighbour effect) is caused by sharing the LLM engine with other tenants. Inference providers serve all customers from a shared pool of worker instances: one worker instance batches requests from multiple clients, so your request’s execution latency can be dwarfed by a large request from another client.

Overpaying versus renting a dedicated instance

At some point, it may become cheaper to rent dedicated GPUs from an inference provider, instead of paying per-request. With a dedicated setup, customers pay a fixed monthly fee per GPU and can calculate a break-even average number of tokens per minute at which dedicated GPUs are cheaper than API pricing. The formula:

Where:

  • TPM: number of Tokens Per Minute at which it’s cheaper to rent dedicated GPUs

  • NGPU: number of GPUs

  • GpuPricePerMinute: cost of renting a GPU for a minute

  • AverageTokenPricePerMillion: weighted average price of a million tokens using the public API

For example, when paying a blended price of $2.31 per million tokens with Kimi K3, and considering running Kimi on an 8 GPU node that costs $6.25 per GPU per hour ($0.104 per GPU per minute), the break even TPM level is:

6. Stage #2: Configuring dedicated GPU nodes

Once you’ve decided to make the switch, the next step is to decide how to configure the dedicated inference infrastructure. This involves answering a few key questions about models and sizing, and the interactivity versus throughput tradeoff.

Models and sizing

The model you want to run will directly influence the minimum size of an inference node it needs to run on. For example, a smaller model like GPT-OSS-120B can easily fit into a single 80GB GPU card. On the other hand, a large model like Kimi K3 that has 2.8T parameters won’t fit on a single node, and requires two 8 GPU nodes with 1,536GB of total RAM to run and host the KV cache. Running a single dedicated Kimi K3 replica can easily cost over $100/hour, so requires very high utilization to break even compared to the per-token pricing.

Interactivity vs. throughput

When picking an inference cluster configuration, you need to decide where to run your setup on the interactivity-throughput curve. The interactivity-throughput curve shows the tradeoff between overall system throughput and an individual user’s interactivity.

The two important concepts:

  • Interactivity: how fast a single user gets their tokens (tokens per second per user)

  • Throughput: how many tokens per second the system can churn out (total tokens per second)

If you optimize for system throughput, you are maximizing the total number of tokens per second the system can decode. In a high throughput point on the curve, individual users will have lower interactivity. Conversely, if only a handful of users use the system, the individual user’s interactivity will be great, but the system will churn out only a fraction of the tokens per second it’s capable of decoding.

The interactivity tradeoff is caused by the way that decoding works in the Transformer algorithm. The decode step generates one token after another. To generate a single token, the GPU pulls all model weights into its core’s memory and runs the decode phase. Most of this is spent waiting on the memory to load while the arithmetic units of the GPU are idle.

You can see the problem: our GPUs are idle while waiting for the memory to be loaded! To work around this inherent inefficiency in transformer architecture, inference engines batch together multiple concurrent requests that require the same model weights. For example, if 50 users are decoding from the same model together, they are all served by the same model weights. Using this trick can increase the system throughput 50x, as long as the GPU has enough compute to make the computations.

This increase in throughput doesn’t come for free, though: each user’s decoding is slightly slower. It’s slower because they wait for all other users’ tokens to be decoded.

At first, the slightly slower performance is a worthwhile tradeoff with batched decoding because the time spent waiting for the weights to be loaded into memory would have been longer, and so the time spent calculating the next token is dwarfed by the memory load operation. For example, Dmytro Dzhulgakov of Fireworks tells us that going from 300 TPS to 100TPS per user makes almost no difference to an individual user, but does increase the overall system throughput by between 5-10x.

As more users are added to the batch, the compute time portion of the overall time spent grows and the tradeoff eventually stops making sense. The shape of the interactivity-throughput tradeoff curve depends on the hardware. The chart below from SemiAnalysis illustrates these trade-offs when comparing two GPUs: H100 from NVIDIA and MI325X from AMD.

When reading the cart, start from the expected median interactivity. Let’s pick 80 tok/s/user on the X-axis. At 80 tok/s/user interactivity, H100 can sustain ~7k tok/sec/chip vs ~2.8k tok/sec/chip for MI325X. Raw performance alone isn’t sufficient for picking a winner, as choosing the right chip also involves cost and availability concerns.

KV cache sizing

When accounting for the necessary inference node memory size, model weights alone are not enough: KV cache has to be kept in the same memory as well. The size of the KV cache is driven primarily by the decision of how many concurrent requests to process in the same batch because each request has its own KV cache. So, a rough calculation for how much memory to process N concurrent requests is:

In this formula:

  • KV size: KV cache size

  • N: number of concurrent requests

  • L: average number of tokens held per request (prompt + output so far). This is effectively the average model context window across all requests currently processed.

  • PerTokenCost: model-specific cost factor per token, depending on the model architecture. Measured in bytes.

Deciding where your setup lives on the latency-throughput curve drives the number of concurrently processed requests. In turn, this contributes to how big the KV cache should be.

High availability, failover, node scaling

All calculations so far have been for a single inference node. But as applications may be used by multiple users, a single node might not be sufficient for all requests in flight. Additionally, for important use cases, it’s good to have redundancy with failover capabilities. Scaling functionality is supported by all major inference providers. Here are the settings that are typically available:

  • Minimum replicas: this is the floor below which a provider will not scale down the number of instances. It typically defaults to 0, so when there is no traffic, a new replica has to be spun up from scratch. Starting from 0 replicas is called a ‘cold start,’ and requests that triggered the cold start are queued until the replica is ready to process them. A workaround to a cold start is to keep the minimum replicas at 1. Keeping minimum replicas at 1 comes with a higher cost: you’re paying for running replicas that aren’t in use.

  • Maximum replicas: the ceiling above which an inference provider will not start up new instances. The main purpose is to limit cost in a scenario of rapid usage spike.

  • Per-replica load targets: This is how the load of a single replica varies across providers. A typical approach is to measure how many concurrent requests a single replica handles. For example, if the KV cache size allows up to 10 concurrent requests per replica, the general guidance is to trigger a scale up when it reaches seven.

  • Scale up/down windows: The time period in which the per-replica load target is observed. The calculation takes the average load per replica over the time window to avoid flip-flopping behaviour.

These parameters are best explained with a diagram:

The red line (left y-axis) represents how many concurrent requests the service is receiving. The blue line (right y-axis) represents how many inference engine replicas are active. In this example, the minimum replica count is set to 0, so when first requests start trickling in, the service experiences a cold start. The load target is set to 70-80% of replica capacity, and when the load target is breached, new replicas are spun up. Once the maximum number of replicas is reached, subsequent requests are queued or rejected. When the number of concurrent requests is down for longer than the scale down window, the number of replicas is scaled down.

Bringing it all together

Instead of trying to work out these questions in sequence, Modal’s Richard Gong suggests working backward from the SLAs. Start with the SLAs that your service must adhere to, which typically involve response times, expected loads, and response quality targets. Here’s a simple model to think about configuring a service:

  1. Choose the smallest model: choose the model that meets the quality target because smaller models are faster to load and hence have more responsive scaling, and are cheaper to run.

  2. Choose the relevant point in the latency-throughput curve. Make this choice based on per-user token latency requirements. It also dictates KV cache sizing and the instance shape.

  3. Configure your scaling settings. Do this based on expected traffic. Min/max replicas allow you to limit maximum spend and cold start problems. Per-replica load targets allow you to tweak how quickly you want to react to changes in load.

If tweaking the settings still doesn’t allow you to reach your response or quality targets, other steps to fine-tune the inference engine are available. Let’s look into decode performance.

With inference, performance improvements can be split into two inference areas:

Prefill optimizations: with prefill, all input tokens are processed in parallel and its performance is strictly limited by computational performance. Therefore, most performance improvement opportunities lie in improved raw hardware performance and optimizing GPU kernels. Modern GPU kernel libraries are very efficient, so performance improvement opportunities in that space are becoming rare.

Also, most optimizations in this area are model-specific, whereas decode optimizations like speculative decoding can be applied to all models, which is why many providers focus on decoding. In Modal’s experience, improving GPU kernels adds a few percentage points of performance for a specific model, whereas improving the decoding performance improves decode throughput for all models.

Decoding optimizations: the main bottleneck with decoding is the fact that tokens are generated sequentially. Speculative decoding improves performance by trying to guess more tokens at once.

7. Speculative decoding

The decoding phase is memory bound: to generate one token, the GPU has to read all of the model’s weights, plus the cached attention state, the KV cache. But with only one new token to process, each weight loaded into the GPU’s memory only gets used in a single, small calculation. That’s not an efficient way to use limited memory on a GPU!

If we’re short on memory but have compute available, why not use the underutilized arithmetic cores (the idle compute) to generate more tokens in a single pass? This approach is called speculative decoding and generates multiple draft tokens very quickly. These tokens are then fed into the LLM that verifies them all in a single pass, similar to how prefill works. The LLM can accept or reject draft tokens and generate at most a single new token in a single forward pass.

In the diagram above, the main LLM accepts two out of three draft tokens, and rejects the last draft token, replacing it with the correct token. Since two thirds of draft tokens were accepted, taking the extra time to run speculation is worth it. In general, speculative decoding makes sense if the speculator can guess more than one token correctly, on average.

Token acceptance is a key metric for the speculator. The higher the token acceptance rate, the more effective the speculator is in a given scenario. To get a sense of how much more effective speculative decoding is, Fireworks’ Dmytro Dzhulgakov tells us that verifying 15 tokens per pass is only 50% slower than generating a single token. This means that as long as the speculator can guess two or more tokens correctly on average, then attempting to guess more tokens is worth it.

The Speculator component can be implemented in a few ways:

  • A smaller model from the same family. A book written by the Baseten team, ‘Inference Engineering’, suggests the Speculator model needs to be at least 10x faster than the main model for the speculation time to be justifiable. It’s important for the model to be from the same family because the speculator and the LLM need to share the token vocabulary. The smaller-model technique is no longer employed by most state-of-the-art implementations because other techniques are faster.

  • Some techniques like DFlash run a separate, specially-trained model that reads the main LLM’s hidden layers as inputs. DFlash always guesses a fixed number of tokens ahead, starting from the last token accepted by the main model. DFlash starts from the main LLM’s hidden layer and guesses tokens independently of each other, enabling DFlash to guess multiple tokens concurrently. A smaller model would still run decoding token-by-token. As a result, DFlash generates drafts much faster. DFlash has been improved upon with techniques like DSpark that further increase speculation accuracy. Improving speculators is a very active area of research in LLMs!

  • Various use-case specific heuristics like n-grams or prompt lookups sometimes work very well. These lookup methods are essentially searching for subsequences of the prompt to predict what token typically follows next. These cheap-to-run techniques tend to work well on predictable content like code.

Most providers offer customization of speculators to customers, although some take different approaches. For example, at Fireworks, they optimize speculators for all dedicated deployments behind the scenes, without customers even knowing it. At Modal, this is a per-request service. Everyone starts with a strong custom speculator which can be further tuned if needed.

The performance gains which vendors report include inference throughput improvement of 20%-50%, with draft token acceptance rates going as high as 10+ in some specialized cases. Speculative decoding does not affect TTFT latency as that metric depends on prefill performance.

Speculative decoding makes sense when there is unused compute during the decode phase. When using shared inference – where requests from multiple different customers are batched together – speculative decoding strictly adds latency. That’s the main reason why providers only offer speculative decoding on dedicated deployments. This is customer-owned capacity that’s frequently underutilized, so can offer improved single-task performance.

Read more about how Speculative decoding works in ‘Why is Speculative Decoding Fast?’ by Joe Barrow.

Speculative decoding is a match made in heaven for coding use cases. It turns out that coding is far more predictable than human languages and even simple speculators that just look at statistical token co-occurrences can accurately predict long token sequences. Such simple speculators are very fast to run, so the extra penalty of running speculators is minimal. It’s one more reason that coding is such a profitable and efficient use case for inference!

Takeaways

This was an extensive deepdive – and yet, it feels like we’ve only touched the surface of many areas.

There’s plenty to get up to speed on with inference engineering, and us software engineers will need to do so. Inference engineering decisions will be made by those who build large-scale backend systems, so it’s worthwhile tech professionals getting up to speed.

Some of the best resources we’ve found happen to come from inference vendors – and are free!

  • What is inference engineering? A deepdive. Our first deepdive on the topic, from March

  • Inference Engineering by Philip Kiely: a free-to-download ebook by Baseten

  • GPU glossary by Modal: an online, interactive ebook, though not one that can be downloaded

  • Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System by Aleksa Gordic: an in-depth explanation of vLLM internals. Great coverage of details like decoding, batching, and scheduling.

The cache is a key part of inference engineering. Much of inference engineering is about optimizing spend, much of which can be reduced by using the KV cache. So, understand how it works, learn about caching techniques, and go deep down to the hardware layer; such knowledge will be valuable when tweaking setups.

Evals, evals, evals! A strong set of evals is a must-have for running your inference. It might be useful to see evals as “unit tests for LLM workloads”:

  • You need them to decide which model to use

  • …to decide whether to upgrade to a new set of models

  • …to get a sense of cost characteristics

Without a strong set of evals, you’ll make production decisions blindly.

If latency is critical, you’ll want to run on your own GPUs. You lose all control over latency when using an API solution, whether from a frontier lab or inference provider, as API serves multiple tenants and you’ll have no control over ‘noisy neighbours.’ If you have latency-critical use cases – like realtime audio, where the target is sub-500ms responses on the p95 – there’s no other option than to run your own GPU within an inference provider, or buy your own GPU!

All this is open source and you can run it. Most of the things in this deepdive will run on our laptops today. Sure, it may not be stellar performance, and smaller models that fit on a single computer may be unavoidable – but it will run. The tools we use in this article (and in the appendix) like llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and many other key components, are all open source.

We hope you found this deepdive useful. Thanks again to the companies which took part for sharing their data and insights. If you have useful resources for learning more about inference engineering, or have personal experience of running your inference, leave a comment below!

Leave a comment

Appendix

The deepdive got long enough as is: but we could have kept going! In the appendix below we’re leaving three more examples and interesting parts about inference engineering:

  1. The impact on cold cache vs hot cache: an example

  2. An aside: KV cache is why inference is so profitable for vendors

  3. Speculative decoding in practice

#1: The impact on cold cache vs hot cache: an example

Let’s run this example on a locally hosted model with the llama.cpp inference engine. Both calls are identical, but the first one hits the endpoint with a cold cache, whereas the second call is completely served from the cache.

Looking at the timings response field: it took just 200ms to process input tokens for the second request, but more than 16 seconds to process the first request. Notice that the response generation (predicted_ms field) is roughly the same: prompt caching only impacts processing of input tokens. The phase where the LLM processes input tokens is also called the ‘prefill’ phase.

You should start measuring your cache hit ratios. In the context of LLM serving, a simple approach to define the cache hit ratio is to express it as cached_tokens / prompt_tokens:

  • cached_tokens is the number of prompt tokens fetched from cache

  • prompt_tokens is the total number of prompt tokens, including those for which prefill ran

If the cache ratio goes down, you should investigate if something changed in the way LLM prompts are generated in the context layer.

#2 An aside: KV cache is why inference is so profitable for vendors

Charging for KV cache hits is why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI can offer such “generous” deals with Max plans – while still turning a profit! It’s an open secret that the Claude and ChatGPT Max plans offer 10-70x as much usage than if you used API billing: for a $200/month plan, you could be using $2,000-14,000 in equivalent API costs. But how? It’s thanks to hosted inference providers charging for KV cache reads. As Diogo Almieda, cofounder and CEO of Typesafe, and creator of Jev, explains:

“Frontier models are more of a commodity than ever, open-weight models are on the rise, and yet the labs’ reported inference margins keep climbing. How?

The answer, of course, is the KV cache (+ the agentic change of workload): more tool calls means more cache reads, which means more profit.

It also explains the “subsidized” subscription plans. SemiAnalysis found that the $200/month Claude plan can yield up to $8,000/month of API-equivalent tokens, and OpenAI’s up to $14,000/month. At list price that’s a 40-70x subsidy, which sounds insane, until you remember that 90%+ of a coding agent’s tokens are cache reads and the true cost of serving them is a small fraction of the sticker price.

[KV cache usage] is also why, if you run agents at scale, self-hosting makes way more sense than it does for chat. Self-hosting an open-weight model is the only way to keep the cheapness of the KV cache for yourself rather than handing it to the lab. At least until cache read prices fall further. Fable 5.1 cut them from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens, which suggests they will keep dropping.”

Diogo’s suggestion on how to optimize your inference spend – pay attention to the number of tool calls:

“The economics of agents come down to one question: how many times does the context get read, and who pays what for each read.

If you build agents, measure your cache hit rate and the number of tool calls. The number of tool calls matters way more than the number of tokens per call. And if you run agents at scale, consider self-hosting to keep those cache savings for yourself.”

#3 Speculative decoding in practice

Let’s see speculative decoding in action. We’ll execute two tests:

  1. Running regular local inference on Gemma 3 12B parameters model

  2. Running inference with speculative decoding for the same prompt

We’ll focus on measuring the token throughput and draft acceptance rate. Let’s first start with running the vanilla Gemma 3 12B parameter model with Llama.cpp:

The command line interface (CLI) above shows we ran the 12B weights version of the Gemma 3 model, quantized to 4 bits. The model was previously downloaded from Hugging Face and after startup, it listens to a local endpoint on port 8080. Let’s now query that endpoint with curl:

The curl command calls the OpenAI-compatible endpoint that llama-server exposed and sends it a few parameters:

  • The prompt: “write a Python function…”

  • Temperature is set to 0 for fewer random results in the test

  • Max_tokens is set to 512 because we don’t care about the actual output in this experiment, only the performance numbers

The server response includes JSON-encoded field timings which is then output through the jq utility for parsing JSON from the command line. The interesting field in this response is predicted_per_second which is the tokens-per-second metric we’re interested in. Without speculative decoding, the Gemma 3 12B model served from llama.cpp outputs ~28 tokens per second.

Let’s now try the same setup with speculative decoding turned on:

In this command line, we added the -hfd parameter to add the speculator model, and chose the Gemma 3 270M parameter model. It’s from the same family and shares vocabulary with the 12B parameter version, but should be significantly faster as it’s much smaller. We also specified that the speculator should speculate at most four and at least one draft tokens. Let’s see how it performs on the same curl call:

We can draw two significant conclusions from this experiment:

  1. The endpoint generated ~40 tokens per second with speculative decoding, so the throughput from the same hardware for the same prompt was roughly ~48% higher.

  2. The speculator drafted a total of 617 tokens, out of which 356 were accepted. The model generated a total of 512 tokens, 356 of which were draft tokens that were accepted. Since the main model always generates exactly one token per pass, we can conclude there were 156 passes, implying that on average 2.3 draft tokens were accepted per pass.

item.title: How Instacart Uses LLMs to Make People Buy More
item.author: ByteByteGo <bytebytego@substack.com>

How Instacart Uses LLMs to Make People Buy More

ByteByteGo
Nov 16
 
READ IN APP
