When people search for a product on an e-commerce platform, they rarely ask for it using the exact words that are present in the product catalog. For example, users might ask for something like “bread no gluten” or “x-large zip lock”.

A good search system is one that is able to look at these phrases and link them to the actual products the user might be interested in. This first step to do so is called query understanding (QU). The job of QU is to take the words the user has typed in a search box and find out useful information about the user’s shopping intentions.

In this article, we’ll look at how Instacart used LLMs to build a product search that could accurately understand a user’s shopping intention. Here’s what we’ll cover:

  • The problem with Instacart’s initial approach

  • How a general LLM becomes useful for Instacart

  • How Instacart made sense of the query category

  • How Instacart made sure that something is always suggested to the user

  • Extracting details from the query

  • How to make the query understanding process much faster

Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.

The Problem With Instacart’s Initial Approach

You can separate product search into 3 broad activities:

  • First, you have QU, which is meant to understand the user’s request.

  • Second is retrieval, where you find a set of relevant products.

  • Third, you have the ranking phase in which you decide the order in which each product is shown to the user.

As you can see, information created during the QU phase is the one that guides both retrieval and ranking. For example, let’s say you have a search query that says “bread no gluten”. It refers to bread with a gluten-free attribute. This search phrase gives a very important piece of information to the search setup if you don’t treat the phrase as three unrelated words.

At Instacart, the QU phase can produce three types of information. First is the product categories, in which you decide which sections of the catalog are important for answering the query. Second is alternative queries, which deal with other search phrases that might help find suitable products. Third is structured tags. This deals with the parts of the query that might help learn more about the product, its brand, or specific attributes.

Instacart already had machine learning systems that helped it understand queries. The problem was how to get it to work consistently for the enormous variety of things that people search for.

One way to solve this problem is to analyze search behaviour. But this behaviour provides imperfect training data. A supervised machine learning model learns from examples that are paired with desired answers. For classifying queries, you might connect a search phrase to the correct product category.

However, as you might have already noticed, it’s quite difficult to collect all these labels. Instacart can look at searches, clicks, and final purchases. But those actions don’t directly reveal whether the system understood the query in a correct manner. For example, you might have a user who searches for bread but ends up buying bananas. Now, this purchase doesn’t mean that “bread” should be classified as a query about fruits. Of course, behaviour can give some nice evidence, but a relation between a query and a purchase decision can be quite noisy.

You can use human reviewers to provide cleaner labels. But this also needs time and money. Also, rare queries have very little history. For example, the user might make a very specific query such as “2% reduced-fat ultra-pasteurized chocolate milk”. If you have a system that learns mostly from historical clicks and purchases, it might not have enough examples to deal with such phrases.

These uncommon searches are part of the long tail. While each such query may account for little traffic, together they might represent a large collection of customer requirements.

Broad queries also create a different type of problem. For example, let’s say you have a search phrase such as “healthy food”. It can point to so many categories, and the system has to handle ambiguity rather than force the query into a single narrow interpretation.

With separate models, you also end up with a lot of maintenance work. Instacart had to maintain different systems for different tasks. For example, they had a category classifier that used a FastText model. The query rewrite system mined patterns from user sessions. Each system needed its own data processing, training, and deployment requirements. This increased maintenance work. And even then, they made inconsistent interpretations of the same query.

Therefore, the Instacart engineering team wanted something that could improve their QU and also provide a more consistent foundation for taking care of the other responsibilities.

How a General LLM Becomes Useful for Instacart

A large language model (LLM) starts off with a broad knowledge of language and the general world. This makes it pretty good at making sense of queries it might have never seen before in the historical data.

For example, an LLM might already know that something like “Italian parsley” and “flat parsley” refer to the same thing, and “curly parsley” can act as a substitute. This is all part of the model’s general awareness that it got during training, and it doesn’t need to learn these things from a bunch of examples.

Of course, general knowledge doesn’t automatically make the LLM knowledgeable about Instacart’s product catalog and the behaviour of their customers. To bridge this gap, the Instacart engineering team used the following techniques:

First, you provide all the relevant information in the prompt to the LLM. This approach is known as context engineering. RAG is the primary method that is used over here. The system pulls in information such as the catalog records and historical patterns and puts that information along with the query.

To be clear, RAG here means that you try to give the model all the useful business information before asking the model to make a prediction.

Second, the system validates the model’s output. Instacart has implemented post-processing guardrails to check how suitable the output is and how compatible it is with their product catalog. You can have a model generate a plausible answer, but it still doesn’t fit the actual data of the business. Therefore, validation is a separate part of the system.

In the third technique, they fine-tune smaller models on their own examples. Fine-tuning means additional training that can change the parameters of the model. Instead of giving all the domain guidance using the prompt every single time, the team teaches the model to work on a particular task with high-quality examples.

How Instacart Knows What the Query Is About

Instacart has organized its catalog using a hierarchy of categories. For example, you have the following path:

Meat → Beef → Beef Ribs → Short Ribs

Each step in this category path makes things more specific. If the search system knows the entire path, it can easily identify the relevant part of the catalog.

The earlier version of the classifier treated these categories more like a flat collection of labels. For example, in the case of “buttermilk”, it might predict “Dairy” and “Milk” separately, where each label came up with a confidence score. While those predictions were also useful, they didn’t express the full relationship.

With the new approach, you combine historical evidence with LLM interpretation and also check the relevance of the product.

In this approach, the system first finds the leading categories that are associated with purchases following the query. These categories form the initial set of candidates. The advantage is that this gives the model a starting point linked with Instacart’s own data. Since typical purchase behaviour can be quite erratic, you need to assess the candidates even more.

In the next step, you ask the LLM to assess the candidates. The LLM re-ranks the candidate categories using the query and the Instacart context that was given to it. For example, “buttermilk” might map to Dairy followed by Milk and then Buttermilk. On the other hand, something like “vegan roast” might map to Meat followed by Meat Alternatives.

As you can see, this is how language understanding and knowledge of the world help understand a query whose wording doesn’t directly match a category name.

Next, they check whether the prediction is relevant. After the LLM makes a prediction, a guardrail compares the meaning of the original query with the predicted category path. This part is done using embeddings, which are numerical representations of text. If the query and the category path get a similarity score that falls below a specific threshold, the system throws away that pairing.

To summarize, the three stages have different responsibilities. Historical data is meant to propose candidates. The LLM’s job is to interpret them. And at the end, the guardrail filters irrelevant results.

How Instacart Makes The Queries Stronger

Even if you have a system that understands a query well enough, the original words that make up the query may retrieve very few useful results. This is where query rewriting helps.

Query rewriting generates alternative phrases that can help the search process find more candidates.

The older search system at Instacart did this using patterns found in user sessions. But it covered only about 50% of the search traffic. The Instacart engineering team initially tried asking an LLM to generate rewrites using a general prompt. But this didn’t work as expected because just asking the LLM to rewrite the query doesn’t tell the LLM what kind of alternative would be useful.

For example, let’s say you have the query “1% milk”. Rewriting might change the query to “one percent milk”. While the meaning stays the same, it does very little to help the user find an alternative product.

To make things more effective, Instacart separated rewriting into three tasks:

  • First, they use synonym rewrites that try to express the same request using different wording. “One percent milk” illustrates this relationship.

  • Next, you have broader rewrites that attempt to get rid of some specificity. For example, “milk” can be a broader rewrite of “1% milk”

  • Last, you have substitute rewrites that suggest a different product that might be a good alternative. For example, something like “2% milk” can act as a potential substitute.

You might think that these differences are pretty minute, but they change the search approach in different ways. When you broaden a query, you make the constraints less rigid. Making the suggestion of a substitute product changes the requested product. A synonym keeps the intended meaning intact.

Each type of rewrite gets a dedicated prompt with specific instructions and examples. They also give it reasoning guidance. Instacart then applies a bunch of post-processing checks and semantic filters.

This approach increased rewrite coverage to over 95%, with more than 90% precision across all three types.

Extracting Search Tags from the Query

The third task is semantic role labeling (SRL). SRL deals with taking out structured concepts such as the product, brand, and other features from a user’s shopping query.

For example, let’s say you have a query that says “2% chocolate milk”. It contains a product “milk”. It also talks about the fat content and flavor. If you represent these concepts explicitly, they become easier to use in the search process.

Instacart uses these tags for retrieval, ranking, advertising, and filters. The main challenge is to find the accurate tags without making every search slow and costly.

One way to do so is by processing frequent queries in advance. Search traffic has an uneven distribution. You might have a relatively small collection of frequent queries that take up a big share of the traffic. These are known as head queries. Beyond them, you can have a much larger collection of uncommon or previously unseen queries.

For these types of common queries, Instacart can generate tags ahead of time and save the results in a cache. Subsequent searches can use those tags immediately.

However, you cannot have the system precompute tags for every possible phrase. New combinations keep coming up, so caching needs a companion process that can deal with queries with no pre-existing result.

To handle this, Instacart used an offline teacher pipeline and a smaller model that runs at the time of live searches. The job of this offline teacher is to create high-quality examples. Here, “offline” means that this work takes place outside the live request flow that the user is waiting for. Due to this, the pipeline has more freedom to use a powerful model and richer context information.

For a common query, it can find relevant information from internal systems, provide that information to the LLM, generate tags, and validate the tags against the catalog. For example, consider the search phrase “verdant machine”. Without business context, an LLM might think of this phrase as talking about machinery. However, Instacart’s internal evidence connects this query with a smoothie brand called MuchPure and with other smoothie juice categories.

The output validation serves two purposes. It helps populate the cache for common queries. Also, it becomes part of a training dataset for the smaller model.

This is why the large-model pipeline is called a teacher. The outputs generated by this model become examples from which another model learns.

When a live query comes in, the system checks whether tags are already cached. If they are, it returns them. If they are missing, the query goes to the smaller, fine-tuned model.

The student has already been trained on examples generated by the teacher pipeline. It learns how queries should map to structured tags, including patterns present in Instacart’s domain context.

Teaching the Smaller Model

For its real-time SRL system, Instacart fine-tuned Llama-3 8B. This is a model with approximately 8 billion parameters.

For reference, parameters are the numerical values a model learns during training. Although 8 billion is still a pretty big number, this model is a lot smaller than the larger frontier model used by the teacher pipeline.

Instacart trained it using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation). In LoRA, you make a model learn a relatively small set of additional parameters while keeping the original model weights fixed during fine-tuning. This brings down the amount of training work you need to adapt the model.

The training examples all depend on the offline pipeline.

This process is a form of knowledge distillation. In this, you have a smaller model learning from outputs generated by a more capable teacher model. Based on their analysis, they found that the student generated fewer incorrect tags. But it also missed slightly more correct tags.

How Instacart Made the Model Fast For Live Search

For a high-traffic website like Instacart, you want the search system to respond quickly enough so that users don’t face long delays.

The Instacart engineering team targeted model-serving latency in the low 100s of milliseconds. Its initial setup took nearly 700 milliseconds on an A100 GPU.

Several changes made this possible.

One of them was merging the LoRA adapter into the base model. After training, the LoRA adjustments can be combined with the base model’s weights. This prevents the need to keep the adapter as a separate computation during inference. According to the Instacart engineering team, this adapter merge brought down latency by about 30%. After they combined this with an upgrade to H100 GPUs, they were able to achieve the 300-millisecond target.

Therefore, the total improvement came from both a change in how the model was served and faster hardware.

The team also tested FP8 quantization, which uses lower-precision numerical representations for model computation. This brought down the latency by another 10%, but recall declined slightly. Instacart chose to deploy the unquantized model because they wanted to give more priority to higher-quality results.

You can think of this as an engineering trade-off. Though a faster model was available, the team made this choice.

They also reduced how often live inference is needed. Caching had a large effect on the overall cost. According to their estimate, only 2% of queries required real-time model inference.

Therefore, the smaller model handled a limited amount of traffic, while cached tags served the common cases. Instacart also used GPU autoscaling to run fewer GPUs during quieter periods.

Conclusion

Instacart made an evaluation of the real-time SRL system through A/B testing. For the tail queries discussed we talked about earlier, it reported a 6% reduction in average scroll depth. You can interpret this as users finding the right items more quickly.

The system was also dealing with millions of cold-start queries each week. These were the queries for which the system didn’t have query-specific history or a precomputed answer. There was also a 50% reduction in user complaints related to poor search results for tail queries, with only a marginal latency increase.

As you can see, these stats connect the problems to the solutions. Better classification, rewrites, and tags help shoppers find relevant products more easily. As part of further developments, Instacart aims to understand a shopper’s broader journey. The current design lays a strong foundation for that direction.

  • Building the Intent Engine

Software engineering after code becomes cheap with Satya Nadella

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on AI’s impact on software engineering, code verification, hybrid cloud+local models, and engineers’ careers.

Gergely Orosz
Nov 16
 
READ IN APP
 

Listen and watch now on YouTube, Apple, and Spotify. See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom.

Brought to You by

• turbopuffer – a ridiculously scalable, fast and cheap hybrid search engine, built on top of object storage, used by cutting-edge companies like Anthropic, Linear, Ramp and many others. Many companies that switch to turbopuffer are cutting their search bills by 50% or more and getting much faster results. Check it out. Also, check out the new and improved The Pragmatic Engineer search I built on top of turbopuffer!

• Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature for reviewing PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It also supports stacked PRs. Check it out

• WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules, and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Learn more

In this episode

What does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part?

There can be few people in tech more qualified to tackle this hot topic than Satya Nadella. Microsoft’s CEO started his career as a software engineer – a rare thing among Big Tech CEOs. Satya joins me to discuss how building software is changing at Microsoft, and what it means for us, software engineers.

We start with Microsoft’s embrace of open source from the mid-2010s and the lessons learned from building VS Code in the open. I ask how Microsoft went from holding an early lead with GitHub Copilot to having to catch up with Cursor and Claude Code, and what it reveals about building products around rapidly improving models.

Satya also explains what a “software factory” means to him, why specifications and verification are becoming more important, and how teams that work on products like the Windows operating system are adapting. We also touch on Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers, AI-related anxiety around engineering careers, and hear Nadella caution against drawing long-term conclusions from the slowdown in junior hiring.

We also explore open and local models, why companies need to control their own AI infrastructure, and how to build safeguards around increasingly capable agents. Satya also has some advice for engineers who want to excel during this period of change – and why he would like to spend more time on building.

Sidenote: we recorded this episode in Redmond just a few hours before Microsoft’s day-long Outlook outage, so there was no discussion of it. To the people asking: no, I did not pull out any cables during my visit that might have kicked out that outage :) However, I am already talking with the team inside Microsoft on-point for this outage, and expect a more detailed follow-up in the newsletter on what went wrong and what we can learn from it.

Takeaways from the conversation with Satya

I appreciated how grounded and thoughtful Satya was – and how pragmatic he is in suggesting to verify anything and everything related with LLMs, and not blindly trust anything or anyone (including vendors or AI models!) 12 of the most interesting takeaways I noted:

1. A new form of software engineering: teams building software factories to improve their work. Satya cites the Azure networking team which manages 500+ fiber network operators and recently built an agentic system to better manage emails and processes. Now, they operate much more efficiently as a result. Satya sees this as the reality of “AI transformation”: brownfield work on building software factories to improve how teams operate, all while continuing the day-to-day work.

2. GitHub Copilot fell behind Claude Code because the IDE faded out in just six months. Dev tools are in Microsoft’s DNA, but it was completely unprepared for Claude Code retiring the concept of the IDE in favor of the command line. Satya admits this move by Anthropic caught them off guard, and it taught him that when a non-linear model jump occurs, the form factor of using that model can change fast. He also admits the IDE “faded away” over the course of just six months, and Microsoft’s stronghold in dev tools had been the IDE, with VS Code. It sounds like Microsoft learned a lesson here and is now more nimble with dev tools, and less attached to past form factors.

3. “Own the intelligence”: avoid lock-in & treat agents as an insider risk. Satya cautions companies to avoid lock-in with any single model provider by ensuring that the harness, memory, and model are not coupled, so that they can be changed with ease. He also thinks more companies should consider using open models as a way to protect their core intellectual property (IP) from leaking out, and build private evals to decide what models to use and upgrade to. He also says that models are intelligent but unreliable, so it’s best to treat them as “insider risks” and build a separate system to verify that agentic systems work as expected.

4. Microsoft is betting on “hybrid intelligence.” Satya questions why we rely on the cloud for AI infrastructure when last year’s frontier-equivalent model can already run on a laptop, while the frontier-equivalent model from as recently as the previous quarter can run on desktops. He predicts the concept of “hybrid intelligence” will gain traction, of having local AI models running on laptops and desktops, and a model router deciding when to use cheap, “unmetered” local models, and when to route to a more capable, expensive one in the cloud. Microsoft is building infra to support such routing with its Microsoft AI (MAI) models and Surface Laptop Ultra lineups.

5. Code generation has become cheap, but verification is still hard. Satya reveals he’s been thinking a lot lately about how challenging it is to verify the correctness of code generated today. Models doing a “critique” on generated code is one solution, but it involves model alignment issues, such as a model achieving its goal in undesirable ways; for example, making tests pass by deleting failing tests. Satya also thinks we’ll start to build more verification loops based on production traces, in a kind of “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). But for this, models need to be able to verify fixes, meaning we return to the verification problem! We didn’t arrive at any definite solutions for this during the conversation, which tells me this is a problem space that will keep many of us engineers busy!

6. What’s with those voluntary exit offers? I asked Satya directly why Microsoft recently made voluntary exit offers to most of its software engineers for the first time in the company’s history. I also wanted to know if it could mean layoffs in the future. Unsurprisingly, his reply was diplomatic, and my more direct interpretation is this:

  • Large transformations/reorgs are likely because teams will change in size (many getting smaller) and function, with many new AI-related teams being formed.

  • There’s high demand internally for new, AI-related roles like forward-deployed engineers.

  • A voluntary exit offer can motivate engineers who feel “stuck” on their current team (for example, if there’s less opportunity to do AI-related work) to take interviews elsewhere, and, with an offer in hand, depart with a smaller “bonus.” Satya admits that even inside Microsoft, not all teams got the memo about becoming more AI-native. Those affected can accept a voluntary exit offer until December, and it’s safe to assume many are indeed interviewing at other places!

  • There is a lot of change ahead. My take is that any “pre-AI” company will have to restructure itself, not just Microsoft. At least Satya is candid about it.

7. The cause of the junior hiring slowdown is that companies are figuring out the new way to work. I asked if Microsoft is hiring new grads and juniors, and Satya admits there’s a slowdown there (and at many places). He identifies a process that’s currently taking place as the reason why:

  • There’s an internal reorg happening on team sizes and roles

  • Teams are figuring out how to build “software factories” and how to balance human cost/effort and token budgets

  • When all this is figured out, then junior recruitment will pick back up

At Microsoft, most teams are busy coming up with new ways of working, so it’s not a good time to bring in new hires. Satya expects this “reorg” phase to be temporary, after which hiring will pick up.

8. Microsoft has started a “preceptorship” program for AI-accelerated development. In collaboration with Carnegie Mellon University, Microsoft launched the PRAISE program (Preceptorship for AI-accelerated Software Engineering). It’s actually a concept borrowed from nursing, where new nurses are paired with experienced ones to develop real-world experience and confidence. Preceptors are experienced software engineers who coach “preceptees” on using AI tools thoughtfully, while building strong systems thinking, taste, and judgement. This is the kind of program I wish more companies would consider partnering with educational institutions on; perhaps this one will inspire other engineering leaders.

9. The next big engineering challenge: building “software factories” within teams and companies. Satya believes every company needs to control their AI infra – the harness, context, memory, model – and that verification of the generated code is a hard, currently unsolved, problem. Inside Microsoft, he sees lots of teams building their own “software factories” to improve team and org operations. As we talked, it became evident that building software factories looks set to be a widespread engineering problem across the industry because it’s a novel challenge without many existing “blueprints”. It will be slightly different for every team and company. There’s going to be lots of work in this space!

10. “Migrating” to AI is quite different from migrating to a new technology. We talk about how “migrating” to become “AI-native” feels similar to a brownfield project introducing a new technology, such as moving over from HTML+JavaScript to React. Satya also perceives some differences:

  • All tools are changing, not just a single technology: the runtime, the framework, and the concept of the IDE

  • When a new model launches with new capabilities, it can invalidate existing setups, just as models like Opus 4.5-and-above have invalidated IDEs.

11. Satya is very enthusiastic about decision models. Satya loves how decision models like ‘Jev’ and Microsoft’s ‘Decision-1’ are a kind of new primitive. He says: “These decision models are kind of like Excel macros. What happened to spreadsheets with macros can happen with code with intelligence embedded as a primitive. This primitive has a distribution, it doesn’t need to be generated again and again, it’s token-efficient. I think that this is one of those places where software engineering remains very much alive. Decision models are like the stored procedure of the intelligence era.”

12. Satya’s advice for winning with AI: stop reading & listening about it, and start using it more. He says:

“It’s ironic on a podcast to say, but it’s “do more, learn more, and be hands-on.” Experience it firsthand. If I could change the ratio of my “talk” to “do,” I would. This is the time. If there’s one piece of advice – whether you’re mid-career, a CEO, or a fresh college grad – it’s that the more you can take the time to learn, to be in teams that are doing it, then the better that is versus anything else I can think of.”

item.title: Announcing .NET 11
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Announcing .NET 11

.NET Team

.NET 11 is now available with improvements across the full stack, including C# 15 union types, faster SDK tooling, and hundreds of runtime optimizations. ASP.NET Core gains async validation and OpenAPI 3.2, while .NET MAUI moves to CoreCLR as its default runtime. The release also adds built-in AI development tools, including an MCP server template and new Blazor components for building agent-powered apps.
item.description: Announcing .NET 11

item.title: Device bound session credentials in ASP.NET Core
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Device bound session credentials in ASP.NET Core

Maarten Balliauw

Session cookies work like keys: steal one and you own the account. Maarten argues DBSC fixes this by tying a session to a private key locked in the device's hardware, so copied cookies expire fast and can't be refreshed without a signature only the device can produce. ASP.NET Core added server-side support in .NET 11, but it was pulled before release for being incomplete. The plan is to rework it for .NET 12.
item.description: Device bound session credentials in ASP.NET Core

item.title: Packing algorithms in C# from boxes to restaurant bookings
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Packing algorithms in C# from boxes to restaurant bookings

Scott Galloway

Packing problems share a common challenge: having enough total space doesn't mean everything will fit. Simple strategies like first fit and best fit work well for one-dimensional bin packing, but adding physical dimensions, irregular shapes, or time makes the problem harder. Scott points out a restaurant booking system shows this clearly: free time scattered across a schedule cannot simply be added together, and a table must meet capacity and accessibility rules before availability even matters. Finding valid placements first, then ranking them by preference, keeps the logic clean and failures easy to explain.
item.description: Packing algorithms in C# from boxes to restaurant bookings

item.title: File-based apps in .NET 11: Room to grow
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
File-based apps in .NET 11: Room to grow

Barret Blake

.NET 11 expands file-based apps, letting you write and run a single C# file without creating a full project. You can now split code across multiple files using directives, reference existing libraries, and manage NuGet packages directly from the command line. Tools like dotnet package add and dotnet reference add work straight against a .cs file. When a utility outgrows this approach, one command converts it to a standard project.
item.description: File-based apps in .NET 11: Room to grow

item.title: Convert string to integer
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Convert string to integer

Khalid Abuhakmeh

C# offers three ways to convert strings to integers. Khalid suggests using int.TryParse for untrusted input because it returns a bool instead of throwing exceptions, using int.Parse only when input is guaranteed valid, and Convert.ToInt32 when null should equal zero. He warns to watch out for culture and formatting issues, as strings like "1,304" need explicit number styles and culture settings to parse correctly. And the most popular article from the last issue was: * C# 15 collection expression arguments: What's new vs C# 12 and 13 ( https://csharpdigest.net/links/23701/232e01d9-4af9-4c0c-9aef-e9d370f900fa/email ) ----------- newsletters -----------
item.description: Convert string to integer

item.title: engineering
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
engineering

Brian Houck

10 minutes by Brian Houck Brian shares five recent papers that, read together, tell a consistent story: AI is speeding up code writing, but those gains shrink sharply by the time software actually ships. The bottleneck has moved downstream to review, verification, and integration. Developers are losing flow and cognitive clarity even as their output grows. The deepest risk is eroding shared understanding of systems, a form of debt that is easy to miss but hard to recover from.
item.description: engineering

item.title: It was never obvious. Start anyway.
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
It was never obvious. Start anyway.

Yew Jin Lim

9 minutes by Yew Jin Lim Starting a career today feels uncertain, but it always was. The difference now is that skills can become obsolete within a single product cycle. Yew suggests focusing on two things: building genuine craft through repetition and obsession, and finding real problems that need solving. These feed each other. Skip chasing predicted hot skills, optimize your first job for learning over salary, and build real human connections instead of sending hundreds of resumes into the void.
item.description: It was never obvious. Start anyway.

item.title: Automating immersive reading
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Automating immersive reading

Shane Friedman

17 minutes by Shane Friedman Storyteller matches ebook text to audiobook audio automatically, even when chapters are reordered or missing. It first uses a speech model to generate a rough text transcript of the audio, then finds matching text chunks between that transcript and the ebook to locate chapter boundaries. From there, a Viterbi algorithm efficiently finds the best frame-by-frame alignment between the audio and text, pinpointing the exact timestamp of each word and sentence.
item.description: Automating immersive reading

item.title: Do not ask "Is A a B?": Inheritance and the Is-A trap
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Do not ask "Is A a B?": Inheritance and the Is-A trap

Denkstein

12 minutes by Denkstein Experts have warned against overusing inheritance for decades, yet deep and tangled class hierarchies remain common. The root cause is a flawed rule taught in almost every programming course: use inheritance when one thing "is a" kind of another thing. This sounds intuitive but fails in practice, as a mutable square cannot truly substitute for a rectangle even though geometry says it should. Instead, ask whether every promise the base type makes still holds for the subtype, and whether both types will stay tightly linked over time.
item.description: Do not ask "Is A a B?": Inheritance and the Is-A trap

item.title: Database indexing isn't magic
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Database indexing isn't magic

Sushant Dhiman

12 minutes by Sushant Dhiman Database indexes work like a book's table of contents, letting the database jump straight to relevant data instead of scanning every row. Adding an index on the right columns can cut query time from several seconds to milliseconds. However, indexes slow down write operations since the database must update them on every insert or update. Indexes also don't always help with reads, especially when a query returns a huge number of rows spread across disk. And the most popular article from the last issue was:

Where did your agent’s tokens go?

Every retry costs tokens, and the cause can be a slow API or database, not the model. In this live workshop, you’ll see:

Save your spot for November 17 at 10am PT.

Register now

This week’s system design refresher:

  • Kubernetes Explained for Busy Engineers

  • Single Agent vs. Multi-Agent Architecture

  • The Testing Pyramid

  • How LLMs Use AI Agents with Deep Research

  • Common types of AI Agents guardrails on production

Kubernetes Explained for Busy Engineers

Kubernetes is an orchestration platform that manages the deployment and maintenance of containerized applications, particularly on multiple machines.

Let’s see how kubernetes creates and keeps an application running.

  • You describe the desired state of your application in a deployment.yaml file.

  • The API server validates the deployment and stores this desired state in etcd. The etcd is a persistent database that stores the Kubernetes resources, like the number of replicas, existing pods and nodes, and their assignments.

  • The controller manager job is to run controllers and ensure that the desired state matches the actual state of the Kubernetes cluster. For example, when a Deployment requests four replicas, the controllers ensure that four Pods are created and maintained.

  • The scheduler decides where each pod is supposed to run. It assigns the pods to the worker nodes based on the available CPU and memory resources, placement rules, or any other constraints.

  • The worker nodes are the ones that run the assigned pods. Each worker node contains a container runtime that downloads the image and actually runs the container. The kubelet keeps track of the node-to-pod assignment and ensures they run properly.

  • Once the pods are running, the Kubernetes Service provides a stable endpoint to the pods.

The Ingress or Gateway then exposes that Service to the external users.

Single Agent vs. Multi-Agent Architecture

Some tasks need a single agent. Others need a whole team. Knowing the difference is the skill.

Single-agent system: One reasoning LLM that plans, picks a tool, and loops on its own until the task is done. Use a single agent when:

  • the task is a clear, linear sequence

  • one agent can hold the whole problem in its head

  • you want something simple to build and easy to debug

Multi-agent system: An orchestrator that splits a task into subtasks and routes each one to a specialized agent. Use multi-agent when:

  • subtasks can run in parallel

  • one agent writes and another independently verifies the work

  • the problem is too big for one agent to coordinate alone

Single agents are cheaper and easier to build, but they hit a ceiling on complex work.

Multi-agent systems are more capable and more reliable, but they add coordination cost.

Start with a single agent. Move to multi-agent only when context or reliability become the bottleneck.

Over to you: Are you running single-agent or multi-agent systems in production?

The Testing Pyramid

Testing is the backbone of reliable software. The Testing Pyramid is a widely accepted strategy for structuring tests into three key layers:

  • Unit Tests: These are the foundation of the pyramid. Unit tests are fast, isolated, and low-cost to write and maintain. They test individual functions, methods, or components.

  • Integration Tests: These tests validate interactions between components, such as APIs, databases, and external services. They are slower than unit tests and require more setup.

  • E2E Tests: These simulate real user flows from start to finish across the full system. They are expensive to write and maintain and tend to be slow to execute.

As you go up the pyramid, the cost of test development, execution, and maintenance increases.

Over to you: Which layer do you find most valuable in your testing strategy, and why?

How LLMs Use AI Agents with Deep Research

When you ask an LLM such as Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini to do deep research on a complex topic, it’s not just one model doing all the work. It’s a coordinated system of specialized AI agents.

Here’s how it works:

Step 1: Understanding The Question and Making a Plan

It all starts with the query, something like “Analyze the competitive landscape of AI agents in 2026. The system doesn’t just dive in blindly. First, it may ask clarifying questions to understand exactly what is needed. Then, it generates a plan and breaks the big question down into smaller and manageable tasks.

Step 2: Sub-Agents Get to Work

Each small task gets assigned to a sub-agent, which is basically a mini AI worker with a specific job. For example, one sub-agent might be tasked with finding the latest Nvidia earnings. It figures out which tools to use, such as searching the web, browsing a specific page, or even run code to analyze data. All of this happens through a secure layer of APIs and services that connect the AI to the outside world.

Step 3: Putting it All Together

Once all the sub-agents finish their tasks, a Synthesizer Agent takes over. It aggregates everything, identifies key themes, plans an outline, and removes any redundant or duplicate information. At the same time, a Citation Agent makes sure every claim is linked back to its source and properly formatted. The end result is a polished, well-cited final output ready for use.

Over to you: Have you tried deep research in any LLM?

Common types of AI Agents guardrails on production

  • Input Screening: Every user request is scanned for prompt injection, sensitive data, and off-scope topics before the model sees it. Unsafe inputs return a fallback message.

  • Context Verification: Every user request is scanned for prompt injection, sensitive data, and off-scope topics before the model sees it. Unsafe inputs return a fallback message.

  • Response Generation: The LLM reasons only over verified context.

  • Output Validation: Every response is checked for groundedness, format, and safety before it leaves the system. Failures trigger up to two retries, then a safe fallback.

  • Operational Controls: A final layer enforces limits, logs every call, and routes low-confidence or high-risk actions to humans.

Reliable agents aren’t built on better prompts. They’re built on the guardrails wrapped around them.

Over to you: Which guardrail layer catches the most issues in your setup?

New Units Of Knowledge

Kevin Kelly

“In the past, books were the primary unit of knowledge. When computers came along, knowledge was combined with action, and the shareable unit became software code. The web made the page and the link the unit, and for twenty years knowledge spread hyperlink by hyperlink. Code itself became shareable as packages and libraries that anyone could snap together. Later, mobile phones refined the knowledge unit into the “app.” Tremendous amounts of potential knowledge and action are compressed into a tiny app, which can be shared, bought, and sold.”

#History IndustryTrends

👋 Hi, this is Gergely with a subscriber-only issue of the Pragmatic Engineer Newsletter. In every issue, I cover challenges at Big Tech and startups through the lens of engineering managers and senior engineers.

The Pulse: What can we learn from the Railway hack?

Also: native mobile and frontend jobs are disappearing, how trust helps an “AI-native” engineering team to succeed, Carta starts selling a coding harness, and more

Gergely Orosz
Nov 12
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

The Pulse is a series covering events, insights, and trends within Big Tech and startups.

Today, we cover:

  1. What can we learn from the Railway hack? Cloud platform Railway has published an extremely detailed postmortem about their recent hack in which the attacker likely used ‘abliterated’ AI models (those with no safeguards). Railway has hardened its systems as a result. Also, a competitor tried to benefit from the incident by getting Railway’s customers to migrate – but then got hacked itself in the exact same way.

  2. Native mobile and frontend jobs are disappearing. New data shows native mobile and frontend job listings are down by 50% at leading startups and Big Tech, while forward deployed engineer (FDE) listings have quadrupled in the same timeframe.

  3. How an extremely efficient engineering team works: Superlogical. Mitchell Hashimoto’s new startup is “AI-native” and cares deeply about craft and developer tools. They skip code reviews and commit to main thanks to deep trust between team members.

  4. Industry pulse. Jensen Huang no longer the CEO of NVIIDA, OpenAI buys Pierre Computer, Carta starts selling a coding harness, Meta buys and shuts down Conductor (a T3Code competitor), and Binance hacked with $6.3B stolen after devs were tricked into downloading packages and attending fake interviews.

1. What can we learn from the Railway hack?

Over the past two weeks I’ve talked with several CTOs and founders at infra companies, and in those circles, it’s an open secret that companies are being targeted by what looks like Chinese attackers, using abliterated AI models (those with no safeguards). These attackers seem to only want AI model keys; most likely to sell at discounted rates. “Popping” an infra company and accessing thousands of AI keys can be profitable, so it’s economical to spend heavily on offensive abliterated models.

Cloud provider Railway was one of the several infra providers that was hacked two weeks ago, with customer secrets leaked. The company has released a very detailed postmortem, which is the most in-depth description of how such an attack happens and how fast attackers adapt.

At a high level, this is what happened:

  • Phase #1: Several unsuccessful exploit attempts. On 18 Oct, the attacker created dummy Railway accounts and tried unsuccessfully to get into the company’s systems. The attacks are blocked, but the attacker did not give up.

  • Phase #2: Get Railway’s monorepo code (5 steps in 11 hours). The steps:

    • Attacker finds a vulnerability so they can read files on Railway’s build system

    • → steals build credentials

    • → tries the credentials on several internal systems

    • → accesses a Temporal cluster that stores build histories

    • → finds Railway’s monorepo as a build history and downloads it

  • Phase #3: Gain SSH access to Railway’s cloud environment (4 steps in 10 hours):

    • Scans the downloaded code; tries using old endpoints

    • → Gets a short-lived cloud credential by exploiting a misconfigured OpenID Connect binding in the deploy pipeline

    • → Uses the short-lived credential to pull a long-lived cloud credential

    • → Finds an SSH key with the long-lived cloud credential

  • Phase #4: Get access to customers’ AI provider keys (3 steps in 3 hours):

    • WIth cloud access, they query the production database and access encrypted environment variables. The attacker filters for AI provider keys

    • → Figures out that there’s a key management service that can decrypt the keys, which the attacker has access to with their access to the cloud environment

    • → Calls the key management service to decrypt customer secrets (AI provider keys)

Let’s visualize how the attack unfolded:

I talked with Railway founder and CEO Jake Cooper, who said the attack was especially frustrating because at one point, they were only minutes behind the attacker: it was down to 1-8 minutes that the attack could unfold in the way it did because Railway’s team was alerted to their build system’s credentials being probed on internal systems eight minutes after the attacker started in phase #2. Railway revoked credentials the attacker used to download the monorepo just one minute after the attacker used them:

What makes attacks by abliterated AI models different

Railway’s summary is the first in-depth account of how an attack from an offensive AI model plays out, and there are several noteworthy details:

From the attacker’s side:

  • Stolen code can be exploited within hours by an AI model. If a human got access to Railway’s monorepo, it would have likely taken days or weeks for them to figure out the weaknesses to launch further attacks at. But with AI models, all this is sped up: six hours after downloading the code, the attacker figured out a plan to get access to the AI provider keys, and knew where to look from then on.

  • Abliterated AI models are like bloodhounds: relentless in chasing their goal. The offensive AI model just kept going and going, trying to get access to ever more systems with the sole goal of accessing AI provider keys. It’s hard to imagine such durability by a human in keeping going through hoop after hoop to finally get access to AI keys!

  • Attackers never give up, not even after all doors and windows are sealed shut. Railway evicted the attacker and revoked all the paths they used to get in. But the attacker returned and probed for new weaknesses the same night!

From the defender’s point of view:

  • Storing hashes of customer secrets is a very smart approach. As soon as Railway discovered the breach, they sent over the hashes of AI provider keys to all AI providers, so those providers could cancel them to avoid the attacker draining customer accounts. Hashing allowed Railway to send the keys without knowing them, and for providers to revoke them immediately.

  • Defenders are handicapped by models’ capabilities. Attackers have access to abliterated AI models, while the models Railway has for defense – from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic – refuse to engage in cybersecurity activity, including defensive work. Railway had no access to Project Glasswing during the incident, which would have allowed removal of some restrictions. As of today, Railway does have access, but many infra companies don’t have that privilege.

  • Railway decided to move to a new build system, instead of patching the existing one. Once Railway realized that its build infra was how the attacker gained entry, they shut down all builds. This was a problem for customers, given they needed to re-deploy builds with rotated keys! Railway decided to move every customer to an unreleased build system, and not attempt to patch the existing one. Fortunately for Railway, they had the new build system nearly ready to go!

During such an attack, the vendor often has to very quickly choose between “bad” and “worse” decisions. Railway faced a couple of these:

  • To simply notify customers that their API keys were leaked, or immediately notify vendors like Anthropic and OpenAI, sending over API key hashes? Railway did the latter at the risk of upsetting some customers, and even causing unaffected customers’ services to stop working until they created and set up a new API key. The trade-off was that this limited overall financial damage.

  • Should Railway have allowed builds to happen after revoking the attacker’s build system credentials? Allowing customers to do builds would have meant less service disruption, but the attacker could have returned via a slightly different path and stolen the rotated keys. Railway decided to bite the bullet by halting builds and rebuilding its build system in a matter of hours.

Lessons from this incident

I’m impressed by how much Railway has reflected on the structural problems that made it easier for the attacker to succeed, and how the company fixed them:

  • Builds should not run on shared machines. The whole attack started with the attacker being able to attack the build’s isolation boundary (the sandbox on the VM), and getting access to the build machine’s environment. Since that build machine ran several customers’ builds, it had credentials that were valuable to the attacker. Railway has now rebuilt its build stack so that each build gets its own throwaway virtual machine – which is a much stronger boundary than a sandbox on a VM.

  • Add fine-grained access control for all internal secrets. Assume that an attacker will appear within your trust boundary and try to use secrets to get access to internal services. After the attack, Railway rebuilt its CI system to separate out sensitive components, with fine-grained access control. Getting access to important and sensitive credentials now requires 2FA, and even biometrics.

  • Assume that attackers have full access to your source code. The attacker was able to come up with a better plan of attack only after getting access to Railway’s source code. Securing all of your source code is very hard – and might not even be possible in the context of social engineering attacks via an employee. So, design security as if attackers already have full source code access.

  • Decommission old, unused systems. The attacker probed credentials on Railway’s old systems, and although they didn’t get far, they could have found more weaknesses. Following this attack, Railway has shut down old, unused systems.

  • Increase logging and alerting. Even if you do all of the above, an attacker could get access to your systems in unexpected or novel ways. As and when this happens, ensure that you will be alerted for unusual usage patterns, like some services being accessed with invalid or old credentials, unusual internal network activity, etc.

  • It’s essential to respond to suspicious activity within minutes, not hours or days later. Attackers with AI are much faster at hopping between systems than we’ve been used to seeing. Defenders have the advantage that they can spot unusual patterns; after all, an attacker is fumbling around inside an unfamiliar system. But you need to act fast to evict an attacker inside your system!

Seeking to gain from competitors’ problems: what goes around, comes around

There’s an unwritten rule among software vendors that you don’t turn competitors’ outages into a sales pitch to try and poach their customers for yourself.

But Northflank evidently didn’t get this memo. On the day of Railway’s outage, the market rival published a blog post titled “How to migrate off Railway.” The article started by linking to Railway’s security incident disclosure, and explained how to safely migrate to Northflank. In the article, Northflank also boasted about its security capabilities:

“Security controls also include BYOC, workload isolation, network security, and envelope encryption, helping teams manage infrastructure access and reduce exposure.”

The article reads like a naked attempt to grab customers from Northflank’s rival, stating: “Railway got hacked, come on over to Northflank, which is a platform that cares about security.”

Any engineering teams that decided to take the offer ended up getting hacked not once, but twice. Nine days after Railway’s hack, Northflank got hacked in a near-identical way. From Northflank’s incident summary:

“The first known decryption of [customer AI] secrets occurred between 02:39 UTC and 03:08 UTC on 30 October. Northflank received its first security platform alert at 11:43 UTC, and our engineers responded within minutes. The exploit was patched within 60 minutes of notification, and customers were notified within two hours.

Some customers have reported unauthorised use of AI secrets. Please rotate all secrets now, both integration secrets and project secrets, even if you haven’t seen suspicious activity. We recommend starting with AI provider keys, cloud provider credentials, payment provider keys, private keys, and database and other service credentials.

We also recommend reviewing your provider logs for unusual activity. If you have seen unexpected AI usage or spend, contact your AI providers directly, such as OpenAI and Anthropic.”

So, Northflank took nine hours to detect that customer secrets had been stolen, 11 hours to notify customers, and – unlike Railway – they did not proactively notify AI providers to revoke the keys. Objectively, this is a worse response than Railway’s, yet it was Northflank that tried to capitalize on the security outage.

In this particular context, companies would do better to help other players in the market, rather than dunk on their competitors, and indeed, Railway’s CEO texted Northflank to offer support and information about their attack. At first glance, this might appear a bit counter-intuitive to help rivals, but Jake Cooper realized what Northflank’s leadership seems to have missed: that it’s bad for all infra providers if many of them get hacked because customers will stop trusting all infra providers! It’s in the interest of providers to collaborate on this matter and harden their own security. Once they do so, then companies win the market based on features, pricing, and innovation.

Plus, it’s just a very short-sighted way of doing business to try to capitalize on novel security incidents, especially as Northflank seems to have been worse at dealing with the breach than the competitor they went after!

I have no affiliation with Railway or Northflank and struggle to see why Northflank did not remove the article about Railway’s security incident article. One guess would be that it’s a sign the business isn’t exactly thriving, and that they’re ready to try anything to keep things afloat.

2. Native mobile & frontend jobs are disappearing

Fresh data from TrueUp – a platform that scans every open job at Big Tech companies and top startups – shows a massive fall in native mobile and frontend positions, while forward-deployed engineering demand has exploded. This finding comes from fellow Substack writer and product manager, Lenny Rachitsky, in his recent tech jobs deepdive:

In April, we covered the engineering job market and found the same trend of native mobile and frontend positions trending downward and FDE roles headed in the opposite direction:

The big difference is that my data showed the percentage of engineers employed as native mobile or frontend engineers, while Lenny’s data shows the drop in jobs posted with those specializations. Either way, it seems like the writing is on the wall: demand for native iOS, Android, and frontend-only roles is collapsing. It’s likely that folks in these positions are very experienced engineers, and this is a wakeup call to expand their domain expertise and become more full-stack in development work they’re willing and able to do.

Another curious stat: tech recruiter job adverts are at an all-time high – surpassing even 2022 levels:

My personal theory is that recruiter hiring is up so much because nobody can find each other in this weird job market: tech companies are overloaded with low-quality inbound applications, fake applicants pretending to be something they are not, and AI-tailored resumes that just mirror the job advert. Meanwhile, strong engineers struggle to hear back about applications for which they’d be a perfect fit.

Anecdotally, I hear many companies are hiring engineers via referrals or in-house recruiters. For example, I asked Linear cofounder and CTO Tuomas Artman how they make most of their hires: inbound applications have been the minority in Europe, but are more common in the US. Still, the vast majority of engineering hires have come from referrals and outreach by founders and recruiters at Linear. The numbers:

  • US: 39% hired from inbound applications (16 engineers of 41 based in the US)

  • Europe: 20% from inbound (4 among 20 engineers based in Europe)

So, while the spike in hiring by tech recruiters could be a sign that companies are preparing to hire more, my take is that recruitment has simply gotten harder and companies are spending more to hire the right people.

3. How an extremely efficient engineering team works: Superlogical

Mitchell Hashimoto – the cofounder of HashiCorp and creator of Ghostty – is back in the startup game. He has cofounded a startup called ‘Superlogical,’ whose team is building a new type of terminal called ‘Rex,’ which is a ‘durable terminal’ with a server-side component. Basically, your sessions don’t get lost when you close the terminal, and it does all this without a central server. I’m playing around with Rex and find it interesting.

Superlogical is only a few months old and its team members are experienced engineers who care about software craft and are open-minded about using AI as an efficiency tool. Mitchell wrote about how their team works (emphasis mine:)

“First, everyone is trusted to push to main. We do machine-aided code review pre-push and human plus more machine-aided code review post-push. Limited to no PRs.

Second, everyone can cut a release. Our release process is fully automated and when you start a release (for any platform) it triggers a Slack notification and a 15 minute countdown.

The 15 minute warning is a final gate that allows people to review plus collaborate on a changelog. During that 15 minutes, anyone in the company can pause the release rollout. After 15 minutes, the train leaves the station. You can’t override the 15 minutes (except to pause). It gives everyone a chance to step in.

Third, we avoid synchronization through fast remediation rather than through planning. The server and clients on various platforms ship features as fast as they can. We use post-hoc human review and AI-assistance to identify feature mismatches across products (”Windows has support for X and Mac doesn’t.” or “Mac and Windows differ in their behaviors for Y in this way.”).

This avoids expensive “sync” meetings and coordination. We trust that producers of features are mindful of what they’re producing, and we trust that adjacent product lines will self-synchronize quickly. In practice, we see feature parity across platforms within 24 to 48 hours.

All of this works on mutual trust. It ONLY works with mutual trust.

But this is already a markedly different practice than what I would’ve done 15 years ago.”

The interesting thing is that so much of this company’s working style rests on trust: colleagues trust each other to move fast without code reviews or pull requests, and leave it up to individual engineers to decide when to do them. Sure, the team uses AI assistance, but their working style is not about AI, but working as a team.

Mitchell describes this working style in more detail in a detailed post.

4. Industry pulse

Jensen Huang resigns as CEO of NVIDIA

Today, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of NVIDIA, in a swift downfall brought about by allegations he had an affair with a Chinese spy. It’s a big event because NVIDIA is built so much around Jensen; his obsession with detail and winning, and an extremely flat management structure. Jensen resigned a week after allegations surfaced. Here’s how events played out:

  • 6 Nov: The New York Times and Financial Times reported that Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, an AI cloud and data center company in Singapore.

  • 8 Nov: Jensen Huang admits he was unfaithful to his wife and apologizes to her and the company

  • 11 Nov: The New York Times reports a second, romantic relationship with a subordinate at NVIDIA that Jensen had

  • 12 Nov (today): Jensen Huang resigns.

Of course, there’s politics involved: the US had been investigating Megaspeed since October 2025 for allegedly circumventing controls by selling GPUs in China in breach of US export rules. US officials recently confirmed that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy, and the story snowballed from there.

The high-flying executive had little option but to step down given all that context, and his departure is a massive loss for NVIDIA.

OpenAI buys Pierre Computer

There have been three notable startups gunning to build the “GitHub for the AI age:” Entire (cofounded by GitHub’s last CEO, Thomas Dohmke), Cursor Origin (built by the Graphite team, acquired by Cursor, then Cursor acquired by SpaceX) and the Pierre Computer Company.

Last week, OpenAI announced it has acquired Pierre Computer Co. From the sound of it, OpenAI will integrate Pierre’s version control into Codex, and I can see them making code storage available as an additional service in the future. OpenAI itself confirms this is the goal:

“Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.”

Carta sells a coding harness

Carta is the leading equity management platform in the US, and despite not being a dev tools company, the fintech has launched a collaborative coding harness, Evergreen:

Carta built this system for itself in July of this year, and saw a major increase in PR output because of the collaboration. Then, they decided to make it into a product and completed the work of “externalizing” it in only a month or two, at my estimation. Pricing is usage-based: charging per millions of tokens used, on top of the provider’s price.

Carta is the second major fintech to launch a collaborative coding harness as a standalone product, after Ramp did so with Inspect.

One obvious impact of AI is that a lot of non-devtools companies are launching devtools products, because it’s much easier to build and ship such products!

Meta buys Conductor & closes it

Conductor is – or was – an AI dev tool for running and managing multiple coding agents in parallel – like using Claude Code and Codex agents all at the same time. Conductor raised a $22M Series A round back in March, which looked like an indicator that the company was here to stay.

But it’s not, as Meta has other ideas. The social media giant acquired the company and team, and the product is to shut down pretty much immediately. New signups had been disabled since the announcement, Conductor Cloud is becoming read-only tomorrow (Friday, 13 November), and the local service will be shut down next year. Employees will join Meta’s AI team, making this purchase an acquihire where Meta only wants the team and not the product.

The largest competitor of Conductor is T3Code – a similar solution built by the software engineer and YouTuber, Theo Browne. On Tuesday, at a dev meetup in London, software engineer Jorge Cohen – formerly on the React team at Meta – could be heard enthusing about how amazing T3Code is, especially for coding from his new iPhone Duo. Jorge showed me his workflow, and how he’s found T3Code to be much more efficient than both Claude Code and Codex. It’s also possible to use Anthropic and OpenAI subscriptions with it.

I suspect Conductor has been popular with devs and was an attractive business prospect. Meta must have offered an eye-watering amount of money that was impossible to resist.

World’s largest hack: Binance loses $6B

On 29 October, Binance was hacked and $6.3 billion of crypto was stolen from the company’s hot wallets. Based on the incident update from Binance, here’s how the hack unfolded:

  • June: identifying a Binance engineer. Engineer ‘A’ on Binance’s Wallet team installed a Homebrew installer while searching for an AI coding tool. Binance’s security team caught that the package manager was malicious, removed it, and rotated security keys. But the attackers had gained details of Binance’s wallet infra, and details of who works on this team.

  • Sep: fake job interview. Engineer ‘B’ was also on the Wallet team (a detail collected in June) and was invited to a “fake” job interview: an interview loop set up by the attacker. At the end of a challenging series of interviews, Engineer B was asked to download a code assignment. Running that code repo triggered malicious code, unbeknownst to Engineer B.

  • 20 Oct: machine takeover. The attackers had access to Engineer B’s machine and silently took over two more engineers’ machines. One of those machines held a token with deployment permissions.

  • 29 Oct: ready to attack. The attackers deployed a container on one of the engineers’ machines, and got unauthorized access to the internal wallet signing service, meaning they were able to withdraw crypto from Binance’s hot wallets.

  • $6.3B stolen. With the setup in place, attackers moved out over $6B worth of crypto. These transactions are not reversible, so that was that.

Attackers were able to move out billions of dollars so quickly and effortlessly thanks to a 2025 improvement in the Ethereum protocol, called EIP-7702. Before it, every transaction needed to be signed one by one – and doing so would have increased the chance of Binance spotting malicious transactions and halting them. But EIP-7702 allows transaction bundling, and that’s what the attacker did by moving $2.5B of funds in a single, irreversible, bundled transaction.

Binance claims to have frozen around $2.8B of the funds transferred out, but even so, the event is the single biggest criminal heist – digital or physical – in history.

Cryptocurrency is one of the biggest of all targets for attackers due to the potential for such massive payouts as this, and the irreversible nature of transactions. If you own crypto, my advice would be to consider how much riskier holding these assets is nowadays, and to look into more security precautions than are currently in place.

Top Types of Hidden Coupling and How to Deal With Them

ByteByteGo
Nov 12
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

When you create an architecture diagram, you usually try to show the services, databases, queues, and the connections between these different components. With the help of these diagrams, developers can understand how a request goes through the system and how the data flows. We also get to know which components depend on other components.

However, these diagrams cannot show all the things that a component might depend on. For example, let’s say you have two services with separate code and API endpoints. At first glance, you might think that these services are independent. But imagine that whenever you change one service, you need to make a change to the other service as well. Or maybe both of these services talk to the same database whose capacity can be consumed by either service. Perhaps both of them rely on a common logging system.

You can think of these dependencies as hidden forms of coupling. If not handled properly, hidden coupling can have a big impact on the health of your system. Also, it can affect how you change things in your system, or how deployments are done. Or how recovery happens. In this article, we’ll look at the various forms of hidden coupling and how you can deal with them. Here’s what we will cover:

  • The various dimensions of coupling

  • Temporal coupling

  • Semantic coupling

  • Deployment coupling

  • Shared schemas and libraries

  • Observability coupling

  • Shared incidents
